'Ghana was the crime scene': The country leading the demand for slavery reparations
- Published
This year has seen a dramatic change in tone in the global conversation about the transatlantic slave trade.
The demand for formal apologies, debt relief and financial compensation from nations and institutions that benefited from slavery has become increasingly forceful.
In March, a resolution was passed at the United Nations recognising slavery as "the greatest crime against humanity" - though the United States voted against the resolution and every European nation abstained from the vote.
The UK, which alongside Portugal dominated the transatlantic slave trade, has consistently rejected the idea of paying reparations, which is perhaps unsurprising given estimates of what Britain "owes" in damages to nations affected run into many trillions of pounds.
This resistance has not deterred the country that has become the leading voice on reparations: Ghana.
Ghana cannot afford to be silent on ensuring that we hold perpetrators accountable"
It was Ghana that tabled the UN resolution, and in June, a summit on reparations was held in its capital, Accra, with delegates from around 80 countries, who concluded that recompense was long overdue.
"Ghana has always been a pan-African leader. We're the first country to attain independence in sub-Saharan Africa and to prove that it is possible to fight imperial might, and win," Foreign Minister Samuel Okuzeto Ablakwa tells me.
Ghana has been given special responsibility by the African Union to be "champion for reparatory justice" and it is clearly a role the country's political leadership is taking seriously.
In part that is because about 10-15% of the estimated 12 million Africans who were forcibly removed from their homes, torn from their villages, and dehumanised on a scale never before seen, were from what is now Ghana. Even more were shipped from its shores.
"Ghana was the crime scene where these atrocities took place, so Ghana cannot afford to be silent on ensuring that we hold perpetrators accountable," Ablakwa says.
The minister has called for a system of reparatory justice that funds educational grants, venture capital for young African entrepreneurs and research into enduring health issues that some argue may trace their roots back to the severe malnutrition and inhumane conditions of enslavement.
And though he insists that this is not about direct financial gain for African leaders, one of the demands laid out at the recent summit on reparations clearly talked of debt relief and debt cancellation.
He also wants individual institutions that benefited from the slave trade to be held accountable and pay compensation. Among these is the Church of England.
In the 18th Century, the Church's missionary wing ran plantations and owned hundreds of slaves, which helped fund its work across the Americas and beyond.
Many Church of England clergy independently owned slaves, and a recent report by the Church's endowment fund reported the institution made large investments in the slave trade from which it made huge sums of money.
In July, the leader of the Church, the Archbishop of Canterbury Dame Sarah Mullally, visited Ghana in one of her first international visits in the role.
She travelled to Cape Coast Castle, one of the many coastal fortresses that had been run by the British, and where enslaved people were held before enduring the brutal "Middle Passage" to the Americas.
As she toured the dungeons where slaves were held and walked through "the door of no return" through which they were forced before being loaded on to ships, Dame Sarah looked emotional and stopped to pray.
"I felt the weight of the depth of evil that the transatlantic slave trade was. You can't help but be deeply moved by the horrific conditions that people were kept in," the Archbishop said.
She also prayed in a 17th Century chapel that was positioned directly above the dungeons.
"For me that is such a stark illustration of the way the Church was involved in the slave trade," she says. "How can the church have sat above the horrors that were going on below?".
"The Church of England has apologised for the part that we played in the transatlantic slave trade but we've also said there needs to be action that relates to that," Archbishop Sarah said.
The Church has set up a £100m ($135m) social impact fund designed to benefit communities thought to continue to feel the enduring legacy of the slave trade today.
But within the Church, the establishment of the fund has encountered resistance, just as the global push for nations to pay reparations has done.
One of the key counter-arguments centres on the fact that some Africans were themselves complicit in the capture and sale of their fellow people.
But Foreign Minister Ablakwa emphatically rejects this narrative. "I think that there's a strategy to divide and conquer and to create a very contrived confusion," he argues.
He stresses that the entire architecture of chattel enslavement was curated by Western slave-owning powers, who simply utilised local actors to help carry out their plans.
The foreign minister points out that when the laws, insurance policies, and financial architectures of the trade were being drafted, "there was no African at the table".
"We denounce and totally reject those claims that Africans are as guilty and complicit as those who masterminded this whole atrocity," he says.
Yet, within Ghana itself, the conversation around African complicity is far more nuanced, and for some traditional leaders, acknowledging the past is a vital prerequisite part of healing.
King Tackie Teiko Tsuru II, the Ga Mantse, leader of Ghana's Ga people, recently took the step of publicly apologising for his ancestors' involvement in the slave trade.
"I think that the transatlantic slave trade was the greatest crime against humanity, and ancestors also took part as players in that trade," says the king.
The Ga people became middlemen who traded with Europeans. They sold gold, ivory and ultimately enslaved Africans, often those captured in local conflicts, in exchange for the manufactured goods brought mainly by the British and Dutch, including textiles, alcohol and guns.
But the king felt he needed to say sorry not just for his own people's complicity, but the complicity of other Africans too.
"I stand on the same point of apologising on behalf of all traditional authorities and my ancestors and forebears for the part they also played in the slavery of our brothers and sisters.
"It has affected lives and societies up to now, and to be able to go forward, you have to look at your past. It dawns on us to admit our fault and correct it," he says.
The king believes strongly in the need for those who benefited from the slave trade to pay reparations and acknowledges that he, too, needs to commit to making financial amends.
"I believe that it underpins a state of moral courage and credibility."
For the Ga Mantse, admitting fault does not dilute the guilt of European empires; rather, it solidifies Africa's moral standing and sets an example as to how to move forward.
But Ghana is leading the way in another aspect of trying to heal the damage done by the slave trade. The country has run a high-profile campaign inviting the African diaspora - particularly African-Americans - to visit the continent.
It has been promoted as a means of bringing people together in the shared story of their traumatic past, with "reparations" quite literally focussing on "repair" at a very human level.
Yaw Asare, now a Ghanaian PhD student at Howard University, previously worked within the President of Ghana's Diaspora Office, which ran the campaign.
Initially, the gathering of black people from across the globe was, he felt, "a beautiful, profound experience devoid of capitalist motives". But he says in some respects the initiative soon morphed.
"The Ghana Tourism Authority also latched on to it and then used it to enhance their tourism project," Asare explains, saying the initiative started to become less about "repair" and more about hitting tourism quotas.
Asare says the campaign has often viewed the returning diaspora simply as a means of foreign cash flow, raising prices and negatively altering local economies.
"Now (local) people are finding that they cannot afford basic things," Asare says, describing how local Ghanaians were economically sidelined.
More devastatingly, he feels the commercialisation of the initiative overshadowed the deep, psychological work that is desperately needed for locals as well as "returning" members of the diaspora.
"We are dealing with humans, we are dealing with people. We cannot reduce them to, 'come see this site, pay this entrance fee'," Asare says.
He also questions - in an initiative that was partly supposed to be about addressing the trauma of Africans in the diaspora - why they were required to pay entrance fees at the same rates as European tourists at, for example, the coastal castles where slaves were trafficked.
He says all of this means a missed opportunity to address deep-rooted trauma some of which he feels is etched into the very geography and psychology of modern Ghana.
"Go to Jamestown (in Accra), people are huddled together because there is the fear of 'if I live far away, I could be taken'," Asare says, pointing to how centuries-old concerns dictated why people built their houses so closely together.
Jamestown is one of the oldest districts in the city, a community originally built around a British coastal fort where slaves were brought, traded and then sent on ships to the Americas.
For Asare, true reparatory justice must prioritise human connection and healing over financial transactions.
"We have to remove the band-aid and then look at the sore, the gaping wound that's present," Asare says about what he sees as real "reparations". "And see how we can dress it and nurse it and heal".

Nanda Malini, one of Sri Lanka's best known voices of protest, dies at 82
- Published
Nanda Malini, a famed Sri Lankan singer whose voice was seen as a soundtrack to some of the country's political and social upheavals, has died at 82.
Songs from her album Pawana, which touched on social issues and urged people to stand up to injustice, were banned from national airwaves in the 1980s, during a particularly turbulent period of Sri Lankan history.
Her political advocacy continued well after those years, and today Malini is remembered as one of the most prominent figures of the Sinhala music industry.
She died at her home in Nawala, just a few days shy of her 83rd birthday.
Born on 23 August, 1943, in a village in Kalutara, Malini was the fourth in a family of nine children.
She went to school in the capital Colombo, where she won a poetry singing competition in 1956, which was seen as the start of her music career.
In the 70s and 80s Malini became known for her songs about social justice, from satirical lyrics about corruption to rallying calls for Sri Lankans to look past racial and religious divides and stand up against tyranny.
Sri Lanka at the time was undergoing a period of upheaval, as Leftist activists spearheaded an anti-establishment movement, airing frustrations against youth unemployment, social inequality and the elite class.
It was also a time of ethnic tensions, which culminated in the eruption of civil war in the 1983.
Authorities at the time banned Malini's songs from being played by national broadcasters - though that did not stop fans from listening to the tracks and attending her concerts.
Her 1987 album, Pawana, which contained songs about human rights and state oppression, is remembered today as the defining music of those turbulent years.
Her advocacy continued even as the country's political landscape transformed over the decades.
In 2022, as the country saw large-scale anti-government protests amid a spiralling economic crisis, Malini was a vocal supporter of the movement and performed to a gathering of demonstrators.
The months of protests led to the toppling of President Gotabaya Rajapaksa.
The Sri Lanka government has declared a three-day mourning period for Malini, as tributes poured in for the veteran singer.
In a statement on social media, Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake said he was "deeply saddened" by Malini's death and called her a "true musical legend of our time"
"Her timeless music inspired generations of Sri Lankans, young and old alike," he wrote.

A demand has been made to install advanced screening systems in government and private blood banks in Kerala in the wake of reports about the spread of HIV, Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C infections among college students in some parts of the country.
Organisations working for the welfare of patients suffering from blood disorders in the State point out that blood banks across India have relied heavily on voluntary blood donations from college students, considering them one of the safest donor groups for many years. Thousands of patients suffering from thalassemia, sickle cell disease, haemophilia, aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, and other blood disorders depend on regular blood transfusions for their survival. However, reports about the increasing prevalence of viral infections among young donors has turned out to be a cause for concern, says Kareem Karassery, president of the Blood Patients Protection Council, Kerala.
The Collegiate Education Department and Visvesvaraya Technological University in Karnataka recently took steps to conduct integrated health camp for HIV testing and counselling for students in all engineering and degree colleges based on a request from the Karnataka State AIDS Prevention Society (KSAPS). This followed reports about the rapid spread of HIV infection among youth in the 18-35 age group there. According to the KSAPS, the number of infected people in this age group rose from 44,500 in 2023-24 to 66,600 by 2025-26. According to a report, more than 7,000 young people in the 18-25 group in Karnataka have been diagnosed with HIV. Reports of blood transfusion-related infections were recently reported from Haryana and Madhya Pradesh too.
Sources say that there are thalassemia-infected children in Kerala as well who were diagnosed with Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C after blood transfusion. However, they are reluctant to reveal their names. One of the HIV-infected children recently underwent a bone marrow transplant surgery in Bengaluru. Doctors say that the child will take another two years or so to test negative for HIV.
Mr. Karassery says that although the donated blood undergoes mandatory screening, many blood banks in the country still do not have access to advanced nucleic acid testing technology, which can detect infections during the window period — the time between a person getting infected with a virus and when lab tests can find it.
Letter to Nadda
In a letter to J.P. Nadda, Union Minister for Health and Family Welfare, Mr. Karassery said that patients who require lifelong blood transfusions are a vulnerable group. He urged the Centre to launch a nationwide awareness campaign on the prevention of HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C, with special focus on adolescents and college students. Details about blood-borne infections, their modes of transmission, and preventive steps should be introduced in the higher secondary school curriculum. NAT screening facilities should be set up in government and private blood banks across the country. Also, a national policy should be developed to provide adequate financial compensation, lifelong medical care, and rehabilitation support to patients who contract infections through blood transfusions.

A Stubbornly Naive Group of GOP Senators
A small caucus of non-MAGA Republicans keeps falling for the president’s flimsy promises.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
For many observers of American politics, the past few years have been disillusioning, knocking down hopeful beliefs about what the people of the United States will support or tolerate. Even some of Donald Trump’s backers have become disaffected.
Yet somehow, a small caucus of non-MAGA Republican senators has managed to remain preciously naive about the president and the administration he runs. No matter how many times Trump or his aides show who they are and how they operate, these senators seem flabbergasted and saddened.
No case illustrates the ease with which they are fooled like the confirmation of Todd Blanche as attorney general. Blanche was confirmed last week on a 50–49 vote, but only after GOP Senators Thom Tillis and John Cornyn extracted a written assurance from Blanche that a $1.8 billion fund for payouts to Trump allies would not proceed. Senator Bill Cassidy also wavered, but said he was persuaded by the vow. (All three men will leave the Senate at the end of this term: Tillis is retiring, and Cornyn and Cassidy lost primaries to Trump-backed challengers.)
This weekend, Blanche was interviewed on Meet the Press. Kristen Welker asked whether he could “pledge that the Justice Department will always act independently of the White House.” Blanche refused—likely an honest answer, given his demonstrated willingness to follow Trump’s lead, but one that should worry anyone who believes in the rule of law; witness Trump’s repeated demands for political prosecutions, irrespective of evidence. Yet Blanche insisted to Welker that Trump “will never ask me to do something unethical or illegal. He never has. He never will.”
That might reassure someone whose political memory stretches back only as far as early August. But anyone old enough to remember the slush fund, or Blanche’s starring role in negotiating it (as laid out by Federal Judge Kathleen Williams in May), would know that Trump not only has asked Blanche to do something unethical, but that Blanche complied. In order to vote to confirm, Cornyn, Tillis, and Cassidy had to convince themselves first that Blanche’s conduct in that case is not indicative of his basic moral compass; and second that he would be more accountable once permanently confirmed by the Senate than he was when he still had to win over their votes. If Trump finds or attempts to find some way to resuscitate the slush fund—as some experts believe he might—many people will be dismayed, but only this trio of guileless senators will be shocked.
Cassidy’s willingness to vote for a Trump yes-man is all the more puzzling because he voted to convict Trump in his 2021 impeachment trial, and because the president led the charge to defeat him in a primary. (The impeachment vote was Trump’s main reason for targeting him.) But Cassidy has a long record of credulity. As my colleague Nicholas Florko has reported, Cassidy—a physician—cast a deciding vote to confirm Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., but only after the nominee made promises about preserving the existing vaccination regime, a pledge he promptly broke. On ABC’s The Week this past Sunday, Cassidy said “it’s pretty evident” that Kennedy’s vow was a lie. And on CNN’s State of the Union, he called the White House’s latest vaccine move, attempting to unbundle the measles, mumps, and rubella injection, “a crazy, stupid thing.” Senator John Barrasso of Wyoming, another doctor, voted for Kennedy and has since been upset about the administration’s anti-vaccine steps. Who could have foreseen that the prominent vaccine skeptic would undermine federal vaccination policy?
Two other moderate Republicans, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski, voted against Blanche’s confirmation, issuing statements that noted the politicization of the Justice Department under his watch as acting attorney general. But they are not always so clear-eyed. Murkowski delivered one of 2025’s most unintentionally hilarious statements when she cast a crucial vote to pass Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act through the Senate. “My sincere hope is that this is not the final product,” Murkowski said in a statement. “This bill needs more work across chambers and is not ready for the President’s desk. We need to work together to get this right.” Naturally, that didn’t happen; the mystery is why she thought the White House, or Mike Johnson’s House, would improve the bill once she’d surrendered her leverage.
Collins, however, is the dean of the credulous caucus. The Mainer, who faces a tough reelection campaign this fall, is perpetually concerned about Trump-administration actions, but seldom ready to actually use her power. Collins is a rare pro-abortion-rights Republican who previously said she wouldn’t support any Supreme Court nominee who opposed Roe v. Wade. In 2018, she voted to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who said Roe was “settled as precedent.” When Kavanaugh was part of the majority that voted to overturn Roe in 2022, Collins lamented the ruling but now says she didn’t regret her vote for Kavanaugh and would do it again. More recently, Collins helped pass a huge appropriation for ICE with few strings attached, then expressed dismay at the use of the funds to buy “shock gloves” for agents. Even her vote against Blanche was symbolic, because he had enough votes to be confirmed without her.
One could easily write these senators off as cynical, but if they’re acting for political gain, it’s not working well: Cassidy’s and Cornyn’s mild deviations from Trump led to the end of their careers; Tillis’s retirement helped him avoid what might have been a stiff primary challenge. Many of their concerns appear earnest. Perhaps they really just are that gullible, unable to adapt to a Trump age that is leaving them behind. In defending his Blanche vote, Cassidy shrugged off attacks: “I’ll be criticized for this vote. What’s new?” But voters might reasonably expect that their elected officials are savvier about the world than a babe in the woods.

Good morning. After the news about Moderna and Merck’s mRNA cancer vaccine came out yesterday, someone resurfaced a great Sharon Begley story on personalized cancer vaccines from early 2016. I recommend reading it if you’re interested in a primer on “turning your cancer against itself.”
Major cancer group cancels alcohol fundraiser
The American Cancer Society has canceled its upcoming Wine and Spirits Industry’s Gala, a spokesperson confirmed to STAT’s Isabella Cueto. The news came less than two months after Isa and our colleague Lev Facher reported that the group had for years raked in at least $22 million from wine and liquor executives, creating at times an unsettling conflict of interest given alcohol’s known links to cancer.
“Can you imagine the American Cancer Society hosting a tobacco industry gala? This is basically the same thing,” said public health professor Michael Siegel, who called the decision to cancel the gala a wise one. Read more from Isa.
Who is Heidi Overton?
While health secretary Robert F. Kenendy Jr. has been the public face of the MAHA movement and the Trump administration’s health care efforts, Heidi Overton has been the top policymaker behind the scenes, STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo and Daniel Payne report. Now, President Trump has nominated Overton to run the nation’s food and drug agency.
Overton has spent years as a Trump loyalist, having served in the first administration. Some industry leaders are worried about her close association with former director Marty Makary and the White House. On the other side, many MAHA activists are convinced Overton is to blame for stalled and slow-moving policy initiatives. So how might Overton fare at the FDA? Read more.
When hospital chatbots actually come in handy
Modern electronic health records are bloated. As health systems started experimenting with generative AI tools, the idea was that the technology could be used to find a needle in a haystack — the key piece of information, hidden in pages of records, that could explain a clinical mystery and potentially save a patient’s life. Today, a number of health systems are moving toward broad implementation of chatbots for EHRs. But as STAT’s Katie Palmer reports, it turns out that solving diagnostic mysteries is the least of their selling points.
The dominant application of AI chart summarization tools is decidedly less cinematic: Doctors are using them to save time as they prepare to see patients. Still, questions remain about how many errors are worth accepting in the name of efficiency, and ideally, the rare needle-in-a-haystack discovery. Read more from Katie on where things stand.
Inside a 5-year-old brain organoid
For years, scientists at Harvard rented space to the longest-living brain organoids on record. But they rarely actually studied them, as the longevity became an intimidation. “What if you make a mistake and the experiment doesn’t work and all of a sudden you cannot go back to a sample that is so unique?” Paola Arlotta, a developmental biologist in the lab, told STAT’s Megan Molteni.
Eventually, one junior scientist had the courage to analyze the specimens. A study published yesterday in Nature details what the team found. Over more than five years, the organoids had developed and matured in the same way that our own human brains do. Read more from Megan on the science and how it could be used.
Contrasting legal decisions on gender-affirming care
Last week, a federal appeals court ruled in favor of the Justice Department’s efforts to obtain gender-affirming care patient records from the telehealth company QueerDoc. While most judges have categorized such requests as overreaching or for an improper purpose, two out of three judges on the panel ruled that there was nothing out of line about the QueerDoc request. (Some legal experts believe that the case could be a candidate for en banc review, meaning the entire court would review the case again.)
The QueerDoc case was the first of many quashed requests to be appealed by federal law enforcement. But since oral arguments were made in March, the DOJ has taken a different approach to other subpoenas, concentrating its efforts in a Texas district court with a strong conservative reputation. At least one subsequent criminal subpoena, for records from NYU, has been temporarily blocked by a New York federal court.
Most recently, transgender patients and advocates logged a victory in court, as a district court struck down a Trump administration rule that attempted to exclude gender-affirming care from the “essential health benefits” that Affordable Care Act marketplace plans are required to cover. While only a handful of states explicitly include transgender health care in their list of essential benefits, the care is often covered as part of another protected category, like prescription drugs. The judges ruled that the administration did not use proper procedure to propose the change — an argument that probably won’t work against a similar rule barring Medicaid from covering the services.

A 58-year-old man on death row convicted of killing five people in 2009 was executed Friday morning — the first execution under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s administration.
Sunao Takami was convicted of pouring gasoline and setting a pachinko parlor near his home in the city of Osaka on fire in July 2009, killing four customers and a worker at the establishment and injuring 10 others. He was arrested the following day after he turned himself in.
His death penalty was finalized in 2016 after the Supreme Court rejected his appeal for leniency. The defense team had argued that Takami was suffering from a mental disorder and should have limited criminal responsibility.

(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Ramya Kannan writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
Did cataclysmic events happen over the week in healthcare - developments that made us sit up and take note, fume a little, wonder much and record everything? Bringing to you, five major themes that caught our attention this past week, and then, some more.
AI technology is forever invading our columns here, opening up the possibilities of what can happen in the future, and indeed, bringing the future to our door steps today. The last week, there was news about researchers using AI to design, hold your breath - viruses. A particular type of virus actually - a bacteriophage. Infectious Diseases specialist Dr. Abdul Ghafur explains what happens when AI begins to design pathogens. Referring to the Stanford experiment that produced the bacteriophages (bacteria- eating viruses), he explains: “It does not show that AI can casually manufacture dangerous human viruses; it shows that computers are beginning to move from analysing biological information towards proposing biological designs that scientists can physically build. This requires appropriate governance and safeguards.”
“The computer did not create a virus. It did not touch a test tube or handle a living cell. What it did may ultimately be more consequential: it helped decide what the virus’s genome should be,” he writes. Of the 285 AI-generated designs physically synthesised and tested in the laboratory, 16 produced functioning phages. Some were able to overcome bacterial resistance that defeated the original virus. What is new, is not the physical manufacture of a virus. AI has entered the design stage of biology. For medicine, that creates remarkable opportunities. For biosecurity, it raises equally important questions, he says.
Further, in the cardiac diseases sector, AI heart disease prediction tools show promise but are not ready for clinical use, Afshan Yasmeen writes, quoting a review. Published in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making, an open-access journal. The review assessed 30 studies published since 2017 on AI-based models developed to predict future cardiovascular disease among adults without established heart disease. Researchers say “Many models demonstrate good discrimination, but very few studies examine whether the predicted risks correspond to what actually happens in different populations.” For more on this, hit the link above.
From AI, to another cutting edge research segment - genetics. Dr. C. Aravinda and Dr. Veera Rajagopal step into that highly niche area and highly technical area: turning off genes. What we can learn from nature switching off human genes, they ask, based on a study from Pakistan.
Imagine the human genome as an enormous instruction book, they describe, containing the information needed to build, run and maintain the body. Its 23 pairs of chromosomes are like chapters, and the text is written in DNA, using an alphabet of just four chemical letters - A, T, G and C. Within this text, genes are individual instructions or recipes, each made from a particular sequence of these DNA letters. Proteins digest food, transport substances, build tissues, transmit signals and act as the antibodies that defend us against infection. Genetics studies how these instructions are inherited, altered and sometimes naturally switched off.
This is something you might want to read too, if genetics is what floats your boat. D.P. Kasbekar here, writes on how a Hyderabad scientist found out: Scientists find why a debilitating genetic disorder - FRDA - affects only Eurasians.
While at it, do check out this really interesting piece on What can genetics usefully do in your consultation room today? by Dr. Alok Kulkarni. “It can reduce blame. A mother did not cause schizophrenia by being ‘too strict’. A father did not ‘transmit’ bipolar disorder through a moral failing. Biology matters and families often find that acknowledgement to be a relief,” he writes.
Moving on to cancer, we had a comprehensive article on why vital chemotherapy drugs are in short supply in India, with inputs from all the bureaus across the country. India is facing a critical nationwide shortage of two key chemotherapy drugs, cisplatin and carboplatin, driven primarily by the soaring global platinum raw material costs, West Asia shipping route disruptions, and domestic price caps. While government hospitals in several States have managed to stabilise supplies, private hospitals in many parts are still facing a crunch. For patients, this has meant interruptions or delays in life-saving treatment. In response, the government last month raised temporarily ceiling rates for the two drugs by 50%, to help restart halted domestic manufacturing lines. Do read more at the link.
In significant news in the sector, the Supreme Court asks 19 States and UTs to declare cancer as a ‘notifiable disease’ for early detection. This was after it was informed that only 17 of the 36 States and UTs have so far notified cancer as a notifiable disease in light of the recommendations made in a parliamentary standing committee report.
In this podcast, Zubeda Hamid discusses with Dr. Rajeev Jeyadevan about the consequences after Three common medicines were declared carcinogenic. What does this actually mean for patients? The International Agency for Research on Cancer earlier said that three commonly prescribed medicines, hydrochlorothiazide, used to treat high blood pressure, voriconazole, an antifungal medicine and tacrolimus, an immunosuppressant were classified as carcinogenic, or cancer causing, to humans. For the details, click on the link.
This past week, we also featured a number of stories focusing on the gendered aspect of health care. Women with endometriosis are at a 46% higher risk of developing diabetes, a study suggests. Endometriosis causes severe pelvic pain, painful periods and fertility challenges. Researchers, led by those at the George Mason University in the US, followed nearly three million women in the Utah Population Database between 1996 and 2021, including nearly 100,000 diagnosed with endometriosis.
Staying on the subject, Can weather affect your periods? And when should you seek medical help? Athira Elssa Johnson explains that extreme heat, humidity, cold weather and changes in routine can make periods harder to manage. However, persistent changes in cycle length, bleeding or pain should not simply be blamed on the weather; it is important to seek medical attention then.
Continuing our neglected women in science series, I write on Jean Purdy: an unrecognised contributor in IVF, and whose work was critical in the birth of the first test tube baby Louise Joy Brown.
Bindu Shajan Perappadan quotes experts who advise that identifying and addressing health risks in both prospective parents could improve reproductive and pregnancy outcomes, in the article Rising obesity among Indian women underscores need for preconception interventions.
Switching gears to nutrition, recording other top news, Supreme Court slams FSSAI for not introducing front-of-pack warning labels on packaged food products. The Bench went as far as to ask the country’s food regulator whether it does not want children to grow up healthy. “You should be concerned about the health of young children. They are addicted,” Justice Pardiwala added.
Also read this article A timely reset for the Food Security Act, by Dr. V. Mohan, Dr. Soumya Swaminathan, and Dr. Ninja M. Nazar. They write on the significance of the draft National Food Security (Amendment) Bill, 2026 that links Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) entitlements to household size. The policy challenge is to correct inequity without reducing existing foodgrain access, while creating a pathway towards nutrition security, the authors say.

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments - Antonelli out-qualified Russell at the second race of the season on the high-speed Jeddah street circuit and stuck it on pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."

Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says. "We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said: "Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Azharuddeen, Vinil send Ripples through KCL
Left arm pacer T.S. Vinil’s fiery spell upfront and Mohammed Azharuddeen’s blitzkrieg during the chase powered the Alleppey Ripples to an eight-wicket win over Trivandrum Royals in the ongoing Kerala Cricket League at the Sports Hub Greenfield Stadium in Thiruvananthapuram on Friday.
Vinil’s spell in the PowerPlay, which included a double wicket maiden over, broke the back of Royals batting, and it limped to 126 for eight in 20 overs. Azharuddeen (68, 29b, 8x4, 5x6), dropped on eight by Sijomon, sealed the Royals’ fate in the PowerPlay. After his dismissal, skipper Sachin Baby (26 not out) and K.A. Arun (24 not out) guided Ripples home with 43 balls to spare.
A Royal collapse didn’t seem to be on the cards when Vishnu Vinod smoked the first ball of the match from Vinil through covers for a boundary. However, Vinil’s twin strikes in his second over turned the contest on its head. Vinil got the ball to jag back and pinned Vishnu (7) in front and dismissed Abhishek P. Nair for nought.
Royals’ skipper Krishna Prasad felll short while going for a non-existent third run as Royals slumped to 26 for four in the PowerPlay. Sijomon Joseph (46) and K. Ajeesh (23) counterattacked to add 39 runs for the seventh wicket, which enabled Royals to cross 100.
Azharuddeen started imperiously, hitting Vinod Kumar for consecutive boundaries, but Sijomon, at covers, failed to latch onto a mistimed drive from the batter in the same over. Azhar made Royals pay for the grave error and took the game away with his scintillating knock.

In the summer of 2026, a rumor spread that U.S. insurer State Farm, which covers homes, businesses, pets and vehicles, was handing out $5 billion in cash to its automobile insurance customers because the company had strong financial results in 2025.
The rumor appeared on TikTok, Reddit and Facebook. One post on X said some State Farm auto insurance customers could receive up to $100 per vehicle (archived):
Several news outlets reported the story, including CBS News, Fox Business and the New York Post tabloid. In addition, several Snopes readers reached out seeking to verify whether the offer was real or a scam.
As we outline below, the offer was legitimate. State Farm confirmed the plan on its website on July 31, 2026, and created a portal for auto insurance customers to claim their checks.
"Yes, eligible 
The spokesperson went on to say the company announced the plan in February 2026, following strong results for 2025 (we found the announcement on its website):
This dividend is possible due to State Farm Mutual's financial strength and a stronger than expected underwriting performance, which has been reported industry wide. As a mutual company, State Farm is uniquely positioned to provide value directly to customers rather than shareholders. The payments average $100 per vehicle and will vary by state and premiums paid.
On July 31, State Farm said it was starting to issue "dividend payments" to some of its customers. A dividend is a portion of a company's earnings, typically distributed to its shareholders.
"Each customer's payment is based on a percentage of the premium paid for each qualifying policy in 2025. Percentages vary by state, ranging from 4% to 10%," the July 31 announcement said.
The payout concerned nearly 50 million insured vehicles. "Because the distribution covers more than 49 million auto vehicles, the payment process will take several months to be completed nationwide," State Farm said on its website.
According to the spokesperson, customers should wait for a "dividend payment selection email from donotreply@e.sfdividend.com" that will include unique identification and PIN to connect to the insurer's dividend payment portal. The customers will then have the opportunity to select their preferred mode of payment.
For further reading, Snopes has confirmed that several suspected scams were legitimate, including an ATM surcharge settlement.

Areas in Delhi could soon be notified under town planning schemes (TPS), requiring landowners to mandatorily pool their land for planned development, including roads, parks and other public infrastructure. The provision, introduced in the Master Plan for Delhi-2047, which was notified on Thursday, is aimed at taking forward the land pooling policy in areas where owners have not been able to voluntarily come together, a senior Delhi Development Authority (DDA) official said on Friday.
According to the official, the new model will not replace the existing consortium model for land pooling. Instead, it will give the DDA another way to assemble land in smaller pockets of less than 20 hectares that do not form a consortium.
“The master plan roads of 30 metres and above in high-density corridors and low-density areas will be constructed through TPS,” the official said. “If a landowner has one acre and 50% of it is required for a road, the floor area ratio permissible on the one acre can be allowed on the remaining portion,” he said.
The DDA’s land pooling policy covers 105 villages across six zones, and the authority estimates that the areas could eventually unlock land for about 12 lakh homes.
Once an area is notified as a TPS — TPS-1, TPS-2 and so on — participation by landowners will be mandatory, the official said.
“Their plots will be reconstituted after portions are set aside for roads, open spaces, social infrastructure and other services. The features of the land pooling policy concerning outcomes and benefits to landowners will remain the same across the models,” he added.
On a large scale
The move comes as the DDA tries to make its land pooling policy work at scale. The authority stopped acquiring land in 2013 and introduced land pooling under the Master Plan for Delhi-2021, shifting to a system in which private landowners pool their land while the DDA assumes an active role as a facilitator rather than a developer.
Under the existing consortium model, landowners with adjoining plots of 20 hectares or more come together to form a consortium. Forty per cent of the pooled land is given to the DDA for roads, parks and other public infrastructure, while the owners retain 60% for residential and commercial development.
However, voluntary participation has been a hurdle. Landowners representing at least 70% of the land in a sector have to come together before a consortium proposal can be processed. Disagreements, particularly in sectors spread across two or three villages, have delayed the process.
“Farmers coming together on their own to form a consortium can develop the land on a 60:40 basis. But if participation is voluntary, there will always be some who do not join. Then it becomes difficult to develop the entire area or carry out public infrastructure work,” the official said.
Thus, the authority has done away with the mandatory consortium requirement, allowing individual landowners with at least 20 hectares to approach the DDA directly.
Third mode in works
A third mode of land pooling is also being worked out.
“The detailed regulations for the entire land pooling policy will come in the next few months with the approval of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. They will explain TPS and the other modes as well,” the official said.
The DDA has examined models followed in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Mumbai and Ahmedabad. It is also processing amendments to the DD Act to provide for mandatory pooling through TPS.
“The amendment is to make pooling mandatory. At present, the DD Act primarily mentions land acquisition, so we want to clearly provide for the Town Planning Scheme as well,” the official said.
Under the consortium model, 15 proposals are already in the pipeline, while one project has been sanctioned.
“The ultimate benefit to the farmer and the DDA will be the same. The difference is in how the land is brought together,” the official said, adding that the revenue outcome for the authority would also remain the same across the models.

Mahua Moitra moves High Court against arrest warrant issued by Nadia court
Mahua Moitra has moved the Calcutta High Court against an arrest warrant issued by a Krishnanagar court in a remarks case. The plea centres on her claim that parliamentary duties and a pending exemption application were overlooked before the warrant was issued.
Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra on Friday moved the Calcutta High Court challenging an arrest warrant issued against her by a local court in Nadia district over allegedly objectionable remarks.
The Judicial Magistrate of the 3rd Court in Krishnanagar had issued the warrant on Wednesday after noting that Moitra had failed to appear before the court despite repeated summonses. She has been directed to appear before the court by August 28.
The matter was mentioned before a division bench of the High Court headed by Justice Debangshu Basak, with Moitra seeking an urgent hearing. The bench allowed the request and directed that the matter be listed for hearing on Monday.
WHY WAS THE ARREST WARRANT ISSUED?
The Krishnanagar court had summoned Moitra to appear on multiple dates. The court said her repeated failure to comply showed a lackadaisical approach and left it with “no other option” but to issue an arrest warrant.
Moitra, however, has argued that she could not appear because she was attending Parliament and that her exemption application had not been decided before the warrant was issued.
She said the first two summonses required her to appear on August 4 and 12. She was attending Parliament on both dates, while her lawyer could not appear because the Krishnanagar court was under a boycott by the local Bar Association.
Moitra said the third summons directed her to appear on August 18, a day after the lawyers’ boycott was withdrawn. She was still in Delhi, she said, while her counsel appeared before the court and filed an exemption application under Section 228 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).
According to Moitra, the judge instead directed her to appear personally the following morning. Her lawyer later sought a decision on the exemption application, saying she could not travel from Delhi to Krishnanagar at such short notice.
The court then issued the arrest warrant, she said.
WHAT IS THE CASE AGAINST MOITRA?
The case stems from a complaint filed by Chaina Nandi and five others, who described themselves as “peace-loving, law-abiding citizens and housewives”.
The complainants alleged that Moitra made objectionable and derogatory remarks about Union Home Minister Amit Shah, personnel of the Indian Armed Forces and certain Hindu religious beliefs and symbols.
They specifically alleged that she made objectionable remarks concerning the “Tulsi Mala”, a religious symbol worn by many Hindu devotees.
The complainants said the remarks hurt their religious sentiments and those of others who hold the symbol in high regard.
Moitra has now challenged the arrest warrant before the Calcutta High Court, which will hear the matter on Monday.

Five missing after fire in Swiss Alpine town
- Published
Five people are missing and eight others injured after a restaurant with apartments was "completely destroyed" by fire in the Swiss town of Thusis, police have said.
Initial investigations indicate the blaze broke out on the second floor and the cause was still being investigated, according to the Graubünden cantonal police.
The force said it was called just after midnight local time (22:00 GMT on Thursday) and that nearly 100 firefighters responded. The roof had to be opened using a crane after the stairwell collapsed.
The Alpine Graubünden region, also known as Grisons, is a popular holiday destination for both winter sports and summer nature activities in eastern Switzerland.
Fourteen people escaped the building, police said, of whom two were seriously injured, two suffered moderate injuries and four suffered minor injuries.
People were taken to hospitals in Chur, Thusis, Ilanz, and Zurich, it added.
Police and the public prosecutor's office are investigating the cause of the fire.

Powerful earthquake strikes Peru’s southern Andes, USGS says
The latest earthquake comes weeks after Venezuela and Colombia were both hit by destructive quakes
A magnitude 6.7 earthquake struck Peru's southern Andes Mountains on Thursday afternoon.
The quake struck at 1 p.m. local time (18:00 GMT) at a depth of 66 kilometers (41 miles), the U.S. Geological Survey reported. The epicenter was 38 kilometers (24 miles) northwest of Upahuacho, in the Parinacochas province of the Ayacucho region.
Shaking was felt across several parts of southern Peru, including the Ica and Arequipa regions.
Luis Vásquez, head of Civil Defense, told the RPP radio station that “no damage of any kind has been reported so far.” Yony Reyes, mayor of Parinacochas province, also confirmed no damage in the capital, while the Peruvian Navy ruled out a tsunami threat.
Peru experiences regular seismic activity due to its location on the Pacific “Ring of Fire.” A magnitude 7.9 earthquake previously hit the Ica region in 2007, killing nearly 600 people.
Thursday’s quake comes after an earthquake struck Colombia last week, killing at least 314 people with another 262 still missing, President Abelardo De La Espriella said Wednesday.
And in June, Venezuela was hit by twin 7.2- and 7.5-magnitude quakes, which led to a national death toll currently standing at 6,300 people.

Ritzy California beach town outraged after gun store opens up next to a daycare
A group of community members has launched a petition to stop the gun store from opening
Residents of a breezy beach community in California are up-in-arms over the fact that a gun store is opening next to one of the city's daycares.
Goodland Guns announced last month that it was moving next door to Here We Grow Early Learning Center in Goleta , a community of just over 30,000 people located just north of Santa Barbara, California.
On August 3, members of the community rallied in a parking lot adjacent to the daycare. Demonstrators gave statements opposing the opening of a gun store next door, according to SFGATE.
Dan Ashton, the owner of the gun store, and Goleta City Council members also attended the rally to address the concerns of the community members.
Ashton told SFGATE that the store is opening at the new spot despite the outcry. The grand opening is set for September 5.
He told the paper if he could have it his way he'd stay at his current location in Old Town Goleta. He's been operating his gun store from that location for 11 years, but was recently told to vacate by his landlord so they could raise the rent on the property.
That left Ashton scrambling for a new home for his business.
“Finding a commercial location took three years of continuous searching, with regular communications with the city over the last 12 months,” he told SFGATE. “Due to Goleta’s rapid growth and the exodus of businesses from Santa Barbara, commercial and industrial spaces are incredibly scarce—especially for a highly regulated firearms retailer.”
He said he did not have "the luxury of waiting" for the perfect spot to open up.
“Although commercial rent increases in California are capped at 10% annually, this unfortunately seems to be a convenient workaround for building owners," he wrote to the paper. "Small businesses in California are being squeezed out by skyrocketing commercial rents, and this was the only viable location that accommodated the State’s strict operational requirements.”
Ashton said he thought he had some productive conversations with concerned residents at the rally, and said his goal is to be a good neighbor, wherever his shop is located.
“We want to be good neighbors, which is why we’ve proactively implemented feasible solutions in direct response to my neighbors’ input," he said.
That said, some residents of Goleta are still critical of a gun shop operating so close to a children's educational center. An online petition is collecting signatures from concerned residents in a big to prevent the gun shop from opening.
“Our children attend Ellwood Elementary, and live just down the street from this location, walking by it regularly,” a one of the petitioners wrote. “There must be a more appropriate place for this business to set up shop instead of within a high density, family oriented neighborhood adjacent to a wonderful preschool.”
The city's officials confirmed to SFGATE that they're aware of the issue and said they're working on solutions.
“We are going to bring some options back that could lead to a change in our zoning or an ordinance that would put potentially more restrictions where gun stores could be located,” Goleta City Manager Robert Nisbet told the outlet.
The gun store's location and relevant zoning issues will be on the schedule for the September 1 Goleta City Council meeting, Nisbet said.
He noted that even if the city cracks down on where gun stores can be located, it's not likely going to affect Ashton's gun store.
Ashton said he doesn't blame the city for his difficulties finding a viable spot to operate his business, but the state's strict laws regulation businesses like his.
The city was simply doing its job interpreting (although incorrectly at times) and enforcing the incredibly strict California Building Code (CBC) and California Fire Code (CFC)," he wrote. "The real issue is the crushing regulatory environment the State of California has created for small businesses. The state makes it nearly impossible to open, move, or survive.”
The Independent has requested comment from the daycare.

A video (here & here) showing a group of people raising slogans against Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is being shared on social media, with the claim that the incident occurred at the Rajiv Chowk Metro station in Delhi during Independence Day, i.e., on 15 August 2026. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video of a crowd raising anti-Modi slogans at the Rajiv Chowk Metro station in Delhi on 15 August 2026.
Fact: The video is from 20 July 2026, capturing protestors raising anti-Modi slogans during NEET protests at the Rajiv Chowk Metro station. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search of the video’s keyframes revealed that the same clip (here, here & here) has been online since at least 20 July 2026. These posts indicated that the video shows NEET protesters at the Rajiv Chowk metro station in July 2026.
Further research led us to similar videos (here & here) published by media outlets showing the protests at the Rajiv Chowk Metro station. According to reports (here & here), on 20 July 2026, several protesters entered the station, caused chaos, and raised anti-Modi slogans while demanding the resignation of then Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan during the ‘Chalo Sansad’ march. This indicates that the viral video predates August 15 and shows the earlier NEET protests. Moreover, we couldn’t find any credible media reports of anti-Modi slogans being raised on 15 August 2026 at the Rajiv Chowk Metro station.
To sum it up, the viral video showing anti-Modi slogans at Rajiv Chowk Metro station is not from August 15. It is an older clip from the NEET protests held in July 2026.

NASA and Katalyst Space Technologies announced Wednesday they are giving up on a robotic mission to rescue the Swift gamma-ray telescope before it falls out of orbit.
The rescue satellite, named Link, launched July 3 on a journey to fly up to NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, capture it with three robotic arms, and boost its orbit high enough to escape a looming reentry. Link is about the size of a refrigerator, with two power-generating solar arrays and three xenon-fueled electric thrusters to send Swift into a safer, higher orbit.
Katalyst, the startup leading the Swift rescue effort, said Wednesday that “ongoing attitude control issues” will prevent the Link satellite from completing its rescue mission. The spacecraft is still alive, and Katalyst said it will make the most of Link’s remaining capacity, which may still allow it to get near enough to Swift for a demonstration of the satellite’s close-in navigation system.
“While the mission will not have the ending we originally intended, NASA and Katalyst are assessing what milestones remain ahead,” Katalyst said in a statement. “We will continue working to extract technical and operational value from the spacecraft.”
It was a lot to ask
The Swift rescue mission was always risky. NASA awarded Katalyst a $30 million contract less than a year ago to build and launch the Link satellite. NASA said Katalyst had to launch the rescue mission by this summer in order to reach Swift before it falls back into Earth’s atmosphere and burns up.
“NASA should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting.”
NASA gave Katalyst a remarkably tight schedule. It usually takes several years to ready a first-of-its-kind satellite for launch. Katalyst did it in nine months. The timeline forced hard trade-offs, with the schedule driving engineers to tolerate technical risks they might not otherwise accept. Everything seemed to go well during the satellite’s first few weeks in orbit.
That changed in late July when the Link spacecraft suddenly spun out of control. Katalyst hasn’t said what caused the problem, but two of the satellite’s three reaction wheels, used for attitude control, stopped working. There were also issues with cold gas thrusters used for finer pointing control. That left the satellite’s three low-impulse plasma thrusters as the only means of regaining control of Link’s orientation as it zipped around the Earth at nearly 5 miles per second.

Former Liberian vice president charged in drug-trafficking probe
- Published
Liberia has charged former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor with drug trafficking, money laundering and a range of other offences, the country's Justice Ministry announced.
Howard-Taylor, who served as vice president for six years to 2024, was detained before boarding a flight to leave Liberia at Roberts International Airport in the capital, Monrovia.
She was taken to national police headquarters, and has yet to make any public comments about the charges.
The West African country has launched a major crackdown of transnational drug trades, particularly cocaine trafficking, in recent years.
Howard-Taylor is accused of illegally importing, selling and transporting controlled drugs, as well as helping to facilitate drug trafficking.
Police have charged three foreign nationals – two Croatians and one Ukrainian – in absentia as part of their investigation. They are accused of being part of the same network as Howard-Taylor.
Liberian authorities say they are determined to apprehend the foreign nationals, and that they are targeting all parts of the drug-trafficking network: organisers, facilitators and financiers.
In recent months, officials have conducted multiple drug trafficking seizures, with some of them among the largest in the country's history.
She held a senior role in former President George Weah's administration, whose six years in power from 2018 to 2024 was plagued with allegations of corruption and financial mismanagement.
When President Joseph Boakai took over, he pledged to crack down on corruption.
He has also said that he does not want Liberia to turn into a haven for drug trafficking. West Africa is increasingly a major transit route for cocaine trading from South America to Europe.

Joshua fight doesn't look like it will happen - Fury
- Published
Tyson Fury says his fight with Anthony Joshua "doesn't look like it's going to happen" in a verbal tirade against his British rival and promoter Eddie Hearn posted on social media.
The pair had been expected to meet in November in one of the biggest fights in British boxing history, but uncertainty over where the bout will take place has cast fresh doubt over the deal.
Joshua and his promoter Hearn have signed a contract for it to be staged in the United Kingdom, while Saudi organisers are pushing for a move to the United States.
"Doesn't look like they're going to sign the fight and it doesn't look like it's going to happen all because Eddie Hearn and that want more money," Fury said in a series of Instagram stories.
Joshua and Fury have separate contracts with Saudi Arabian-owned Sela. New York's Madison Square Garden is understood to be Sela's preference so that the fight - which will broadcast on Netflix - can cater for American audiences.
On Thursday, Hearn told IFL TV that a list of changes required for the fight to take place in America had been sent to Sela.
Hearn says the main change concerns compensation for Joshua because of the different tax implications of fighting in America.
"In layman's terms, by staging the fight in America, Anthony Joshua receives less money than he would do if the fight was in the UK where he was contractually agreed," he said.
Fury responded by calling Joshua and Hearn "disgusting" and "money-thirsty".
"It is what it is. Same old cliche a decade later. Keep running you little cowards," he added.
In further posts containing expletives, Fury called Hearn a "bag carrier" and criticised Joshua's mindset.
"I'll move on and fight somebody else but just know you never had the guts to fight Tyson Fury, ever, you little coward," Fury added.

Hearn sends list of addenda to Sela

Hearn said it had been approved by Joshua and his lawyer before being sent to Sela.
"We've had no feedback yet," Hearn said, adding that he had not heard from Sela for three or four days.
Reports on Thursday suggested a list of changes had been presented to the Saudi organisers. Hearn claims those reports were based on a leaked email and insists the issues raised in it were not part of the list sent to Sela.
"The addendum does not have one of those points raised in that leaked email," he said.
Hearn did confirm Matchroom held a meeting with Sela regarding money owed to the organisation for previously agreed contracts.
He said those issues, which reportedly included payments relating to darts and snooker events, international promotional fees, the World Series of Darts, the Ronnie O'Sullivan Snooker Academy in Riyadh and money owed to Matchroom from previous boxing events, were separate from the Joshua-Fury contract.
Hearn did not directly address claims that Joshua was still owed money from his most recent fight against Kristian Prenga.
"I'm not going to go into that at the moment. That's a contractual position that will be left for another day," he said.
BBC Sport has contacted Sela for comment.
Fury backs Dana White involvement
The situation has been complicated by the arrival of the Dana White-fronted Zuffa Boxing, which is jointly owned by Sela and TKO Group Holdings. TKO is the managing partner, while White is among the promotion's executive leaders.
Hearn has criticised the push to stage the fight in America.
"The reason that this is happening, to be completely honest with you, is because TKO and Zuffa have basically convinced or tried to convince Turki that this fight is massive in America," he said.
Fury also addressed White's involvement.
"White wants to be involved, he can come on my side. He can be a part of me. Get in, Dana. You want to make the fight, you can come on my side," Fury said.
BBC Sport has also contacted TKO for comment.
Joshua and Fury are two of the biggest names in British boxing and have become crossover stars during their careers.
There has been strong support from within British boxing for the fight to take place in the UK.
Hearn said the importance of staging it in Britain had nothing to do with how many fans could attend.
"It's about British boxing. It's about amateur boxing clubs. It's about kids watching the biggest fight in boxing in our country," he said.
He also highlighted Joshua's history in Britain, including winning Olympic gold at London 2012.
"And more than that, it's about Anthony Joshua wanting to have this fight in Britain where he won the Olympic gold medal, where he won the World Championship, where he absolutely changed the face of boxing forever," Hearn added.
