Eight months ago, I packed my life into a suitcase and carry-on and moved from Canada to Japan. Since then, I've spent time in Tokyo, Osaka, and Kumamoto, living out of short-term rentals.
Because I knew I'd be moving around, I needed to keep my belongings light enough for easy transportation — and, of course, I wanted to leave room for the things I'd inevitably buy along the way.
Going from my two-bedroom apartment, packed closet, and bathroom full of products to a small rotation of outfits, toiletries, and necessities has definitely been an adjustment.
Despite that, I'm glad I downsized my belongings. The experience has taught me to live with a lot less, and I made some pretty good choices about what to bring abroad.
Still, there are also a few things I didn't think I'd need that I'm really missing now.
These are the three things I'm glad I packed — and a few I wish I'd brought.
I did a great job creating a capsule wardrobe.
Before moving, I spent a long time thinking about which clothing items to bring.
I didn't want to use up my entire suitcase, because I knew I'd need room for any new clothes I bought in Japan. I also wanted to be able to mix and match outfits.
Eventually, I landed on two pairs of jeans, a pair of jean shorts, sneakers, waterproof boots, two long-sleeve shirts, two sweaters, a dress, two skirts, four tank tops, and a few jackets.
I love having basic, neutral black-and-white clothes that all pair together, so it's easy to stay functional and stylish without looking like I wear the same thing every day.
I'm glad I brought a folding toiletry bag.
I've always packed separate bags for my makeup, hairbrushes, toothbrush, and all my jewelry.
Instead of doing that this time around, I decided to try a folding toiletry bag, and it's been a total game changer.
Now I can fit my accessories, makeup, razors, and everything else into one place. It folds up easily, fits into my suitcase, and I can just open it up and hang it in the bathroom whenever I'm getting ready.
My portable monitor was a smart investment.
This was a purchase I made specifically for Japan, and I would've had a much harder time using my laptop without it.
I got my first monitor when I was a teacher, and it completely changed how I worked. I always have a million tabs open so I can do multiple things at once, and a second screen makes a huge difference.
My portable monitor is super slim, and it fits easily in my computer bag or carry-on. Plus, it came in handy when I stayed at an Airbnb in Tokyo without a TV — my husband and I used it as a screen so we could play our Nintendo Switch.
I'm definitely glad I brought it, and I plan to keep using it when I'm back home.
On the other hand, I should've packed more of my go-to hair product.
There are a few things I wish I'd packed more of, mainly because I underestimated how expensive or difficult they'd be to find in Japan.
I have naturally thick, curly hair, and I can't just use any product on it. Curly-haired people get it.
I've been loyal to my favorite curl gel for years, and it's the only product I really need after my wash days — but because it's so popular, it usually sells out for months at a time.
I got my hands on some before moving and brought a dupe product with me, but that only lasted a few months. Since then, I haven't found anything similar that works for my hair type in stores.
I've also noticed that curly hair products are significantly more expensive on Amazon Japan. One product I've used as a dupe costs around CA$29 on Amazon Canada, but almost CA$50 on Amazon Japan.
In hindsight, giving up the extra suitcase space for more product would've been well worth it.
Antiperspirant deodorant has been difficult to find.
Back in Canada, I was used to summer days that reached 85 degrees Fahrenheit or more, but I always found the heat somewhat dry. Here in Japan, I've spent time in the Kyushu region when most days were about 95 degrees Fahrenheit with lots of humidity.
When I stepped outside, it genuinely felt like I was walking into a wet wall of heat.
Before coming here, I figured I'd be able to find Western-style deodorant. I tried a few, but found them to be a lot lighter than the products I was used to, and I'd sweat them off immediately.
Luckily, my sister-in-law came to the rescue with a couple of sticks when she visited — but if I had a do-over, I'd definitely pack more.
I wish I'd brought better running shoes.
Before coming to Japan, I bought a new pair of sneakers online. Unfortunately, within a few months of daily walking, they broke down, and I had to get rid of them.
That wouldn't normally be a huge deal, but finding shoes in my size here is pretty difficult. I'm usually a size 9 US, sometimes a 10, and I've found that most Japanese stores don't carry above an 8.
I was able to find my size at Onitsuka Tiger, so that's where I'll probably go for my next pair of runners. Still, I wish I'd either bought two pairs of sneakers or invested in better-quality ones from the get-go.

As USS Lincoln heads home, mental health experts tally the stressors of life at sea
The USS Abraham Lincoln — which has been participating in U.S. military operations in the war with Iran — is now on its way home. The roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard that ship have spent a grueling nine months at sea with little relief.
Reports have emerged of deteriorating conditions — and of deteriorating mental health, including apparent attempts by crewmembers to jump overboard. The Navy has not confirmed those reports and NPR has not independently verified them. "A small number of mental health cases were treated with no loss of life," Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said in a statement last week.
Experts say while the physical circumstances are difficult, a lack of careful and consistent messaging from leadership at the highest levels also contributed to the crews' mental distress.
The USS Lincoln is like a small city, according to Armen Kurdian, a retired U.S. Navy captain who served aboard the aircraft carrier in 2005. The labor aboard the carrier, he says, can be uniquely physical and difficult.
" It takes a toll on your body," says Kurdian. "The plane captains are out there on the flight deck — you know, these 18-, 19-, 20-year-olds lugging these 100-pound chains on their backs in 120-degree weather."
He describes dehydration and exhaustion as pilots have to take off and land on the carriers, sometimes at night and in bad weather, and "then just being mentally prepared to go fly because lives are at stake."
In the off-hours, Kurdian says there is little to no privacy, with people sleeping in crowded quarters.
While difficult, these conditions can be bearable, he adds. But experts say once uncertainty is thrown into this equation, it can push people to their mental brink.
Jack Stuster is a retired behavioral scientist who spent decades studying human performance.
"In conditions of isolation and confinement," says Stuster, "one of the worst things that you could do to the person is to tell them they're gonna come home at a certain time, and then you say, 'No. It's gonna be delayed.'"
Return is overdue
The Abraham Lincoln's deployment was originally scheduled to end in May.
In addition to the Navy, Stuster worked with NASA and scientists operating in small groups in places like Greenland, where return flights home were often canceled at the very last moment — even after their would-be passengers had dragged their duffle bags right up to the flight line.
" People have described to me going out there for the third time … only to be told that it wasn't gonna happen," says Stuster, which caused them "to break down in tears."
Then there's the issue of duration. A three-month deployment is ideal, says Stuster, or even six. At nine months, he says, things start to become untenable.
Dr. Phillip Hunt was for years a Navy physician who deployed on several submarine missions. His background is in emergency medicine, but Hunt says in the Navy much of what he treated was mental health. " I was kind of the father confessor, psychologist, what have you," says Hunt.
With a crew of 5,000 people on a ship, Hunt says it's inevitable that some people will struggle with mental health — even in the best of deployment conditions. "You'd have guys getting anxious. You'd have guys getting depressed."
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth says reports of poor conditions aboard the Lincoln are overstated. President Trump recently called the deployment "not nearly long enough."
Hunt says a lack of certainty or reassurance from leadership at the highest levels can trickle down to impact everyone's mental well-being. "Denial of this unit's deteriorating operational conditions is highly detrimental to the crew's morale," says Hunt. "The result can include anger, anxiety, or eventually mental exhaustion and depression."
Hunt says he blames leadership at the highest levels for the lack of recognition of this hardship.
" I just, I feel so badly for that crew. It's just tragic," says Hunt. "Just thinking about them almost brings me to tears."
If you or someone you know is struggling with their mental health, please call or text the number 9-8-8 to connect with a counselor.

Quota set for visitors to popular Sai Kung coastal trail in first for Hong Kong
Authorities will cap daily visitor numbers at Po Pin Chau section of High Island Geo Trail at 2,000 over several stretches in coming months
Hong Kong authorities will cap access to a popular Sai Kung trail overlooking hexagonal rock columns at 2,000 people per day during several stretches from next month and require real-name registration for visitors, marking the city’s first countryside crowd control measures of its kind.
The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department announced the arrangement on Friday for the Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail, after the proposal was floated in April.
The trail is within the Unesco Global Geopark at Sai Kung East Country Park. No fees will be charged for the bookings or penalties for failing to turn up, at least for now.
“The primary reason for the arrangement is that we realise there are sudden increases in visitor numbers over holidays, and some of the capacity of certain sections is close to saturation,” department director Mickey Lai Kin-ming said.
“Through the reservation system, we hope to achieve organised crowd control and to prevent visitors from over concentrating, as well as to protect the environment and improve visitor experience.”
Lai said the move was aimed at protecting the narrow trail from “excessive wear and tear”, adding the quota would be further reviewed.
The roughly 1km-long (1094-yard) Po Pin Chau trail passes giant hexagonal volcanic rock columns dramatically jutting out from the sea and provides a viewing platform overlooking them.

- The claim that U.S. President Donald Trump aide Natalie Harp is a cancer survivor cannot be independently verified by Snopes. Because Snopes looks for primary sourcing and evidence to rate our claims, we are leaving this claim unrated.
- The rumor stems from social media posts criticizing a senator for referencing Harp while mocking Trump in August 2026. These posts said Harp was a cancer survivor, while other posts argued there's no proof of that claim.
- The claim that Harp had cancer is based on her own accounts of her experience battling a rare bone cancer, which she wrote and spoke about in 2019 and 2020. In Harp's account, she was told she'd have to wait for certain treatment options to be approved before she could continue treatment after failing two chemotherapies and being rejected from a clinical trial for an investigational drug. Harp credits Trump's right-to-try law, signed during his first term, for enabling her to be treated with an FDA-approved immunotherapy drug that wasn't approved for use in treating her cancer.
- Based on the available evidence, much of Harp's experience, as told by her, is realistic and believable. Bone cancers in general are rare and often resistant to chemotherapies. Immunotherapy drugs, which are still relatively new and frequently researched, are a promising possible treatment for many bone cancers. Many such treatments are not yet approved for use for treating bone cancers because the cancers are rare and difficult to treat.
- However, there are a few details, largely in her descriptions of cause and effect, that could potentially be inaccurate, based on our research. For example, she credits Trump's right-to-try law for saving her life, when her description of the drug that finally made a difference for her better aligns with a drug that she would've been able to access through an FDA system that has existed for decades.
- Snopes reached out to the White House by email to ask if it could share details about Harp's history with cancer that could potentially be verifiable, such as the name of the drug used in her treatment. The White House did not answer our questions.
In August 2026, news reporting about one of U.S. President Donald Trump's aides, Natalie Harp, intensified, particularly after Sen. Jon Ossoff , D-Ga., referenced her in criticism of Trump, drawing increased attention to the once little-known aide.
Many conservative figures then criticized Ossoff for referencing Harp, who they said was a cancer survivor, in his attacks on Trump. For example, one X post (archived) said, "Harp is a 35-year-old cancer survivor who works in the White House. Ossoff chose to make her part of an anti-Trump attack because he thought it would score points with the Democrat base and generate attention."
The claim surfaced elsewhere on X (archived) and Facebook (archived). Other social media posts (archived) cast doubt on whether Harp ever really had cancer. Some Snopes readers searched the site or sent emails asking whether it was true that Harp was a cancer survivor.
Harp first rose to fame by sharing her account of suffering from Stage 2 bone cancer and how a Trump-signed "right-to-try" law apparently saved her life. Snopes cannot independently verify Harp's account and medical history, so we're unable to rate this claim true or false.
However, we can compare the details of Harp's account with the current medical research available to get a sense of which details, if any, may sound unrealistic in her story.
Harp's account
Harp's claims about her history with bone cancer came from a LinkedIn blog post she wrote and an interview with Fox News in June 2019, as well as a speech she gave at the Republican National Convention in August 2020.
The LinkedIn post, her earliest public description of her experience with cancer, didn't give any details about the specific cancer she was diagnosed with except that it was rare.
She shared slightly more detail two days later in her appearance on Fox News. Brian Kilmeade, co-host of "Fox & Friends," opened the interview (0:04) by saying Harp had Stage 2 cancer. Harp went on to say her illness was terminal (2:10), Kilmeade Said Harp had Stage 2 of a rare bone cancer (2:18) and Harp confirmed she was "the youngest person in this rare bone cancer" she had (2:52).
The cancer diagnosis is not where Harp has begun any of her accounts, however; instead, she has frequently highlighted a medical error she suffered before that.
"On November 9, 2015 — a year to the day Donald Trump would win the presidency — a nurse mixed up my IV with the deadly substance of sterile water leaving me housebound and searching for care," Harp wrote on LinkedIn. She said her physicians offered her medications for managing pain and even Death With Dignity instead of diagnosing her condition.
On Fox News, she said it took two years for doctors to figure out what was wrong with her. Harp also said in that interview that this medical error is one that "no one has survived" (0:52). At the Republican National Convention, Harp said (0:38) she was a victim of a "notoriously deadly medical error," but survived "only to be diagnosed with a rare and terminal bone cancer." Harp then presented the care she was offered afterwards, which is in contrast to her other accounts in which she described receiving these offerings prior to diagnosis of the cancer.
Notably, the web article Fox News published alongside the video of the interview said Harp "has battled stage 2 bone cancer for most of her life," even though the above descriptions make it sound like her struggles with the cancer developed in the several years prior to that interview.
In all of her accounts, Harp described the available chemotherapies failing to address her cancer and being denied participation in clinical trials. At the Republican National Convention, she claimed (1:22) that no one wanted her in their clinical trials because she'd "make them look bad" after failing the chemotherapies.
Harp said her doctor told her she'd have to suffer through symptoms for either several more months (LinkedIn) or more than a year (Fox News interview, 2:43) for the next round of FDA approvals for the clinical trial drugs she was denied.
She wrote that her doctor did not tell her she had other options, so she went to another doctor who was willing to try a different approach: prescribing an FDA-approved immunotherapy drug for an unapproved use. She credits that experimental treatment for her recovery, and Trump's Right to Try Act for that treatment even though she acknowledged that some may argue it was repetitive of existing law.
Snopes emailed the White House to ask if it could share more verifiable details about Harp's experience, such as which unapproved drug was used in her treatment, but 
Right-to-try law
The right-to-try law Harp credits for saving her life essentially allows patients to access drugs without FDA approval for treatment in specific circumstances. According to the law's text, an eligible patient can consent to the use of an "eligible investigational drug" that has completed a Phase 1 clinical trial and "has not been approved or licensed for any use." The drug manufacturer is allowed to decide it won't permit the patient to access the unapproved drug.
A contradiction between the law and Harp's story immediately jumps out. The right-to-try law applies specifically to drugs that have not been approved for any use, but Harp claimed her lifesaving treatment was an FDA-approved immunotherapy drug being used for an unapproved use.
Such a drug could still theoretically be used to treat Harp's condition under a different process that existed prior to the Right to Try Act: expanded access. Expanded access also allows patients who have exhausted all other treatment options for a serious or life-threatening condition to use an investigational drug instead. Investigational drugs eligible for use in expanded access have not been approved by the FDA "for their specific use."
FDA researchers wrote that the agency has been facilitating access to investigational drugs since the 1970s, and regulations describing the pathways to accessing these unapproved drugs have existed since 1987.
A chart by Triage Cancer, a nonprofit organization focused on practical and legal issues that may affect cancer patients, both expanded access and right-to-try require a physician and the drug manufacturer to approve a request to use an unapproved drug. Expanded access also requires approval from the Institutional Review Board and the FDA, which right to try does not.
FDA data says that between fiscal years 2019 and 2023, the FDA approved anywhere between 97.1% to 100% of expanded access requests, depending on the year and the type of request.
Harp's description of events suggests that her physician, and potentially drug manufacturers, would not approve her request for expanded access. Such obstacles would also to be an issue for Harp under the right-to-try law; based on her story, it sounds like Harp became able to use an unapproved drug treatment because she got a new doctor, not because of the new law.
Comparing Harp's story to actual research
While Harp's story may be vague on specifics such as names and dates, it does have enough details to compare it to reality.
In 2008, the Pennsylvania Patient Safety Authority reported that bags of sterile water were being mistaken for IV solutions because of similar appearance, and that these mistakes were capable of causing serious harm to patients, sometimes even killing them.
It's unclear whether Harp suggested that such a medical error led to the development of her cancer, but in any case, Snopes could find no evidence that such a mistake could cause cancer. According to the Pennsylvania Patient Safety Authority, the IV error is dangerous is because sterile water can cause red blood cells to break down too soon.
Based on the report's description of a patient who survived the sterile water injection, others have survived the medical error that Harp claimed no one else had survived. The less-extreme version of Harp's claim, in which she calls the error "notoriously deadly," is accurate.
Bone cancers are rare in general, and there are many different specific kinds of bone cancers. The American Cancer Society even suggests seeking out clinical trials because these cancers are rare and difficult to treat.
In fact, the University College London wrote that bone cancers are frequently resistant to chemotherapy. The American Cancer Society says that "in recent years" researchers have developed non-chemo drugs, including immunotherapy drugs, to help treat some bone cancers.
The Cancer Research Institute says that while surgery is often the main treatment method for early-stage bone cancers, immunotherapies may be used in treating more advanced or far-reaching forms of the cancer.
The FDA first approved an immune checkpoint inhibitor, the kind of immunotherapy drug often used for treating these cancers, in 2011, according to the Osteosarcoma Institute. (Osteosarcoma is a type of bone cancer.) The institute says no new treatment options for the cancer have been approved in 40 years.
The research above does suggest that much of Harp's story about her battle with cancer is plausible. Bone cancers are rare, so it's expected that whatever kind of bone cancer she'd have would be rare itself. Many bone cancers are resistant to chemotherapy, which would explain why Harp failed such treatments twice.
It also makes sense that the unapproved treatment she and her doctor tried would be an immunotherapy drug. Cancer research organizations point to immunotherapy drugs as a promising avenue for treating some forms of bone cancer. New immunotherapy treatments are still emerging today, and so it wouldn't be surprising if the drug wasn't yet approved 10 years ago.
On top of all of that, the rarity of bone cancers can make it difficult for emerging treatments to be tested with large enough sample sizes in trials to quickly move through the approval process.
For further reading, Snopes has recently fact-checked a number of claims about Harp, including whether an image of her and Trump in a helicopter is authentic.

Four years after Matrimony.com successfully defended its use of the ‘Jodii’ brand, the listed matchmaking platform has suffered a setback in its trademark dispute with ‘Jodi365’ operator Free Elective Network. A division bench of the Madras High Court has restrained Matrimony.com from using Jodii or any other mark deceptively similar to Free Elective’s registered Jodi365 trademark. The August 11 order overturned a July 2022 single-judge ruling that had dismissed Free Elective’s trademark infringement and passing-off suit against Matrimony.com. The division bench also directed Matrimony.com to surrender for destruction all materials bearing the Jodii mark or another deceptively similar mark, including brochures, screen prints, packaging, advertisements, and online material. However, the court rejected Free Elective’s demand for ₹1 Cr in damages, saying the company had not presented oral evidence to establish the extent of the loss it suffered. Matrimony is contemplating moving the Supreme Court (SC) against the order. “Based on legal advice, (the) company is contemplating to file (an) appeal before (the) Hon’ble Supreme Court,” Matrimony said in an exchange filing. How The Dispute Began Free Elective operates Jodi365, an online matchmaking platform whose device mark has been registered since May 2010 across classes covering advertising, telecommunications, and entertainment and educational services. The company claimed that it has been using the Jodi365 mark since 2009 and has built substantial goodwill around the brand. Matrimony.com, meanwhile, launched its matchmaking app Jodii in October 2021 under the BharatMatrimony umbrella. Free Elective subsequently sent Matrimony.com a cease-and-desist notice in November 2021, alleging that Jodii was deceptively similar to its registered mark and could confuse consumers because the two platforms offered similar services. Matrimony.com rejected the allegation, arguing that Free Elective’s registration covered the composite device mark Jodi365 rather than the standalone word Jodi. It contended that Jodi, meaning a pair or couple, directly describes the purpose of matchmaking services and cannot be monopolised by a single company. Matrimony.com also cited several other matchmaking and dating platforms that used Jodi in their names. Free Elective then approached the Madras High Court, seeking permanent injunctions against trademark infringement and passing off, the destruction of materials bearing the allegedly infringing mark, and ₹1 Cr in damages. The 2022 Verdict In July 2022, a single judge bench of the Madras HC, dismissed Free Elective’s suit after finding that the word Jodi was descriptive of matchmaking and matrimonial services. While the court recognised Free Elective as the registered proprietor and prior user of the composite Jodi365 device mark, it held that the company could not claim exclusivity over Jodi as an individual element. The court also compared the two marks and their overall presentation and concluded that the differences were sufficient to rule out a likelihood of consumer confusion. Free Elective subsequently challenged the ruling before a division bench of the HC. Why The Bench Disagreed The division bench disagreed with the single judge’s decision to assess Jodi separately from the complete Jodi365 trademark. It held that Jodi was the distinguishing, prominent, and essential feature of Free Elective’s registered mark and that the trademark had to be considered as a whole. The court also found that Matrimony.com had not initiated proceedings to rectify or cancel Free Elective’s trademark registration. Therefore, it could not challenge the validity of the registered mark as a defence in the infringement suit. On the question of passing off, the bench said the earlier ruling had focused on the visual differences between the two marks without adequately considering their phonetic similarity. It held that Jodi365 and Jodii are deceptively similar and can lead consumers to believe that the two matchmaking services are associated with each other. The bench also admitted additional evidence comprising communications and transcripts or recordings of 11 interactions in which consumers allegedly confused Jodi365 with Matrimony.com’s Jodii. Matrimony.com’s argument that Jodi is commonly used by other matchmaking platforms also failed to convince the bench. The court said the company did not submit evidence establishing the scale, reach, or reputation of the third-party platforms it cited. Consequently, the bench set aside the 2022 judgment and granted Free Elective the injunctions and other reliefs it had sought, barring the damages claim.

Only four in 10 healthcare facilities worldwide meet basic sanitation standards for accessible and usable toilets, the United Nations said on Tuesday (August 18, 2026), while 11% have no sanitation services at all.
In a report, the UN’s health and children’s agencies said only 40% of healthcare facilities last year had toilets that adequately met the needs of patients and staff, including people with limited mobility.
The report from the World Health Organization and UNICEF for the first time provided global estimates of basic sanitation services in healthcare settings.
Its 2025 estimate found significant gaps in access to basic sanitation standards, which it said required usable facilities including at least one toilet dedicated to staff, at least one sex-separated toilet with menstrual hygiene facilities and at least one toilet accessible for people with limited mobility.
Relying on data from 70 countries, the report showed that sanitation levels in healthcare facilities varied widely between regions, with only 23% of facilities in sub-Saharan Africa providing basic services, compared to 55% in central and southern Asia.
It found there was no sanitation service at more than one in 10 health facilities globally, serving 936 million people.
In addition to sanitation, the report estimated access in healthcare facilities to water, hygiene, environmental cleaning and waste management.
It found that an estimated 85% of facilities last year had basic water services, 72% had basic hygiene services and 71% basic healthcare waste management services.
Only 59% of facilities meanwhile met basic so-called environmental cleaning standards, which require both cleaning protocols and trained cleaning staff and is core to infection prevention and control.
A full 18% of facilities, serving around 1.5 billion people, met neither of the environmental cleaning requirements, said the report, which for this category relied on data from 54 countries.
The situation is particularly dire in poorer countries.
The environmental cleaning standard was met by just 24% of facilities in the world’s least-developed nations.

I won’t lie to you: I hated the first digital wall calendar I tried.
I tested it last year and was left unimpressed. It was expensive and massive, and my calendar details were slow to appear (if they appeared at all). The device felt more like clutter than a useful addition to my home. So, I wrote off the idea of using a digital wall calendar, but to my surprise, they have only picked up in popularity and options since then. After trying a few new models myself this year, I can now see why.
These gadgets work by taking your online calendar—whether your Google Calendar, the calendar app on your iPhone, or your corporate Microsoft calendar account—and putting it on a digital screen that you can mount on the wall or prop up on a countertop or table. They’re often more than just calendars, also functioning as chore charts, meal planners, and sometimes even digital photo frames. I usually have smart displays all over my home, especially in my kitchen and living area, but for the past two weeks, I’ve replaced them all with digital wall calendars. And you know what? I don't miss talking to those annoying AI-powered assistants.
Instead, as someone who already lives and breathes by her Google Calendar, I love being able to see it on a large display in the middle of the kitchen, without needing my phone—especially when it’s on a digital wall device that immediately reflects my most up-to-date calendar. My husband and I have also been using the extra features more often, particularly to guide my 4-year-old through his evening bedtime routine with the help of his own companion device. Here's everything you need to know about the best digital wall calendars and whether they're right for you.
Updated August 2026: I've added the Skylight Buddy as a kid-friendly tool that includes some features of these digital calendar devices. I’ve also ensured accuracy and up-to-date information throughout.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
My Favorite Digital Calendars
What’s a Digital Wall Calendar?
You might have heard these gadgets called by various names. Maybe “digital wall calendar” or “smart calendar device.” Maybe you've just heard the name Skylight Calendar, which is a notably popular model right now. No matter what you call them, these devices all do the same thing: replace a paper calendar with a digitized one that connects to the calendar tools you're already using, like Google Calendar or Apple Calendar. The devices let you see your entire family’s schedule in one view, with the ability to update or add to it without needing a phone or a separate account. It also erases issues like unreadable handwriting and forgetting to write down an event you've already scheduled digitally, and its color-coding system makes it easy to see who's on the hook for which activities.
While these are often called wall calendars, you can usually choose to place them on a tabletop. I preferred the models that included a tabletop stand, but I was still able to prop up the ones that only came with wall-mounting hardware during my testing.
What Else Can a Digital Wall Calendar Do?
These devices aren't just calendars; they’re also designed for larger family management. You'll find features to help you plan meals, track to-do lists for multiple people, and earn rewards on a digital chore chart. The Skylight Calendar 2 is a favorite of mine because it includes a photo screensaver, but you'll need to be a Plus subscriber to get that and some of the other bonus features. Basically, you can use these calendars to manage your family's full schedule, chores, meals, and more in a single device.
Is a Digital Wall Calendar Worth It?
I didn't expect to feel this way, but having a physical version of my hyper-detailed Google Calendar in the center of my home has been a delight. My husband and I both check our calendar at a glance while we're chatting in the kitchen, and at the start of the week, we'll camp out in front of it for a few minutes to plan the week's dinners and grocery needs. My top pick, Skylight Calendar 2, actually prompts us to add items to our grocery list based on what meals we picked (if it's a stored recipe, that is).
My husband and I have found it so useful in part because we're both good about adding events to our individual calendars, so now this device can reflect that work. It lets us skip pulling out our phones when discussing plans for the next day or the upcoming weekend.
The Best Digital Calendars
Skylight's calendar is the most popular for a reason. The brand is known for its digital photo frames, and now you can use the same Skylight app to operate any of its three digital calendars: The older 10-inch Calendar ($170), the newer Calendar 2 ($320), and the Calendar Max ($630). The main difference between these is size, but Calendar 2 is the newest model, with improved performance and interchangeable Snap Frames ($30 to $50) you can purchase to change the device's look.
What makes Skylight great is its software. It's easy to use, and it quickly imported my Google Calendar and the wide variety of calendars shared to it, so I could immediately add all of my family's schedules to the device. The left-side menu bar shows all the pages you can toggle between. Calendar, Lists, Tasks, Rewards, Meals, and Recipes are the main areas you'll use; you can also access the Photos, Sleep, and Settings pages from the same menu.
The app and device interface are clean and intuitive compared with other models, many of which feel like Android tablets with a fancy calendar mode added. I was able to easily assign calendars I created on the device to family members. For example, I assigned my husband's calendar to him without needing him to log in or import it, and I could have assigned any calendar I created to my son as well. I also liked that shared events only appear once on the Skylight, but with both of our designated colors added to show the event in question applied to both of us.
Lists and Tasks sound similar, but Tasks are meant to function as a chore chart, connecting back to the Rewards page to build habits and earn the reward you set after hitting a certain goal. The main audience for this is children who are old enough to check the calendar. Lists are for things like your groceries. If you add recipes to the Recipe tab and then add those to your meal plan for that week, Skylight will offer to put the corresponding ingredients on your shopping list.
The downside of Skylight is the paywall. To access some of the best features—meal planning, rewards, photo screensaver, and the in-app AI assistant tool Sidekick—you'll need to be a Plus subscriber for either $79 a year or $8 a month. Having this device double as a digital photo frame makes it worth the cost to me. I love getting to have my two favorite things nearby: photos of my family and instant access to our shared calendars.
The Everblog HomeCal has an operating system that feels pleasantly similar to the Skylight. It has a bit of an Android undertone to it, but it doesn't feel like a giant tablet as much as the Apolosign or Cozyla calendars (both below). Setup was pretty seamless, but there was a delay for the device to update with my calendar invites. It would also take a while for the Everblog to reflect changes I made to my Google Calendar on another device. While it worked well for the most part during testing, I occasionally noticed events missing from my Everblog. It also turned each calendar email account I connected to the device into a separate profile, which was annoying. I could toggle off the extra emails when I was on pages outside of the calendar, though, so I didn't have three profiles for myself on my Chores page, for example.
The menu on the left-hand side is very similar to Skylight's, with options like Calendar, Chores, and Meal Plan. There isn't a recipe section, which I miss, but there is a Fridge section, which lets you track the groceries you already have. Part of why this exists is because Everblog also has a smaller, battery-powered version of this calendar that's designed to attach to your fridge, aptly named the FridgeCal ($249). Still, I prefer the Recipe tab on the Skylight. The Everblog also has a Chores tab, but no additional tab for tracking regular chores or other to-dos separately.
There's a free photo option, but the uploader tool in the app only lets you add one photo at a time. Painful, but I'm sure many would feel it's worth the free price tag. To use the feature, you'll need to go into the settings on the physical device to turn on photo slideshow as your screensaver. The Everblog defaults to pinging loudly at the start of any calendar event, which you can only change on the device, not in the app.
There's a button on the bottom right-hand corner of the screen that will take you to a homepage with an overview of the calendar and chores, and access to other applications like Spotify and Netflix, if you set up your accounts on this device for streaming content. It comes enabled for wall mounting, but you can purchase the Calendar Stand ($39) if you want to situate it on a tabletop, and there's a wooden frame ($99) you can buy to snap on to give it a nicer look.
Apolosign's digital calendar has three sizes: 15.7, 21.5, and 27 inches. It runs Google's Android OS, so it operates very similarly to an Android tablet and to Google's Pixel Tablet, if you've used either as a smart display, as I have. The Apolosign has two modes: Calendar and Android. Calendar mode worked similarly to Skylight. I seamlessly connected it to my Google Calendar, imported over most of my various shared calendars, and color-coded them.
The Calendar mode has a left-side menu bar (you'll have to tap to make it appear), with sections for Home, Calendar, Routines, To-Dos, Rewards, and Meals. The Home page has a two-column design, showing you the calendar on one side and your Routines and To-Dos on the other. You can then tap into any of these sections or check off items directly from the Home page. Apolosign also has baked-in notifications that chime to remind you about calendar events and to-dos, plus phone notifications to let you know how many items are on your calendar that day.
WIRED Reviewer Kat Merck also tested Apolosign, but used Android mode instead of Calendar mode. Android mode allows you to customize widgets and layout, so she opted for a monthly view. This mode also lets you use photos from Google Photos as a background and screensaver. She says it's nice to be able to customize the layout in this mode, but it struggles to sync with other programs, including Apolosign's own app.
I don't like the Apolosign experience quite as much as the Skylight or Everblog, and Kat agreed that this device is not very intuitive and takes a lot of patience to set up. But having no paywall is a huge plus, and many people will feel it's worth getting used to the more Android-style experience to not pay a monthly or yearly fee. But since it's essentially a large Android tablet, iPhone users have flagged on Reddit that they can't two-way sync between it and their iPhone devices. The Apolosign is often on sale for the same price, if not cheaper, than the Skylight.
If you want a version made for kids, Skylight has something along those lines called the Skylight Buddy (8/10, WIRED Recommends). It's not a digital calendar but rather a chore-and-routine display that helps kids visualize and check off their daily to-dos without needing to navigate an entire family calendar.
My 4-year-old loves his 7-inch Buddy, and it really does help get him to brush his teeth and put on his PJs in a timely (well, more timely) fashion now that it's in his room. It also has a night-light and sound machine, but the sounds are limited, and the night-light is pretty dim. So for those capabilities, I'm sticking to the Hatch Baby my son is used to and loves.
Ultimately, this is most useful if you already have and use a Skylight Calendar. That’s because the Buddy can sync to and show designated tasks already on the Skylight Calendar. But even if you don't have the Calendar and just want more of a routine tool or chore-tracker for your child, this is a really good option. There are subscription options to get more features—Buddy Plus is $39 a year, and Skylight Plus is $79 a year. Skylight Plus is what you should get if you have the Calendar, as it unlocks paywalled features for both devices. But I haven't needed any subscription-only capabilities to keep my son excited about and engaged in his bedtime routine.
Others I’ve Tested
Cozyla Calendar Plus 2 (15.6 Inches) for $350: This calendar is similar to Apolosign with an Android-based operating system, but it didn't import my shared calendars, meaning it took more work to set up. It was overall frustrating to navigate and didn't guide me through its tools as effectively as Skylight or Apolosign. While Cozyla doesn't have any subscription fees, its 15.6-inch size is more expensive than both Skylight's and Apolosign's.
Hearth Display for $699: This is another digital calendar and family tool that has a paywall with an affordable Family Membership ($6 a month) but a much higher initial price point. It's only available in a large, 27-inch size, and I found it was slow to load my calendar and also bulky compared to more affordable options.
FAQs
How Do Digital Wall Calendars Work?
Digital wall calendars sync with your existing digital calendar app of choice, like Google Calendar, and display it on the physical screen. There are usually additional tools for recipes, to-do lists, and chores, but each digital wall calendar varies in how you import the information. You may have to manually import it or type the details into the device, but once you get used to the process, the function can be helpful for the whole family.
Will Changes to My Calendar Appear Instantly?
Changes you make on your native calendar app, like Google Calendar and Apple's Calendar, should reflect quickly onto the digital wall calendar device. But changes you make on the device aren't always backward compatible with the native calendar. It depends on the calendar's settings and how the information was shared; I can edit my primary personal calendar on the Skylight Calendar 2, for example, but I can’t edit my work calendar that I shared to the Skylight through my personal. There are also some syncing issues you may run into with the Apolosign, which doesn't two-way sync with an iPhone since the digital calendar runs on an Android operating system.
How Is a Digital Calendar Different From a Smart Display?
Many smart displays look similar to these devices but have an entirely different operating system. Sure, the Google Pixel Tablet has some overlap with the Apolosign and Cozyla, since they all run an Android operating system. But unlike smart displays, digital calendar devices are designed with specific tools to run your family and none of the clutter. You'll lose out on smart-home support, though Apolosign claims you can use Google Assistant on it (that hasn't worked for me so far). On most devices, you'll also compromise on extras like video streaming (you can, however, stream on Everblog). But as someone who uses a smart display regularly, I really didn’t miss it once I switched over to the digital calendar device. I do wish there were a weather-report page, as most digital wall calendars just show the current weather.
Does It Have to Go on the Wall?
No—in fact, most of these devices come with a table-stand option. I only tested in table-stand mode since I had multiple of these devices in my house at one time, but the wall-mounting option is nice, allowing you to keep your tabletops clear. The 15-inch models are great for tabletops, and you may want to consider larger sizes for the wall-mounting route.

Prince Harry and 6 others to learn initial cost of failed Daily Mail case
Prince Harry and six others, including Elton John, are set to find out how many millions of pounds they will have to pay initially to the publisher of Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper following their failed case alleging privacy invasion
Prince Harry and six others, including Elton John, are set to find out Friday how many millions of pounds they will have to pay initially to the publisher of Britain's Daily Mail newspaper following their failed invasion of privacy case.
Following their defeat in a High Court case in London last month alleging malpractice, such as the illegal hacking of phones, the high-profile figures will learn the scale of their exposure to the roughly 34 million pounds ($46 million) in legal costs accumulated by Associated Newspapers Ltd. The losing claimants are believed to be insured for around half that total.
In addition to an initial payment, which could be up to 10 million pounds, they will find out how they will pay the outstanding amount.
The publisher had strongly denied the claims made during the 11-week trial in London, which ended on July 7 when Justice Matthew Nicklin said there had been a shortage of evidence to support the claims and found a possibility that the reporting came from legitimate sources.
Nicklin is due to give his decision on the financial implications of that decision in a written statement at 2 p.m.
Associated Newspapers has asked for more than 9.9 million pounds as an interim payment, while lawyers for the claimants say the interim payment should be just over 7.9 million pounds.
The other high-profile figures behind the case were Doreen Lawrence, the anti‑racism activist whose son Stephen was stabbed to death in 1993 as he waited for a bus; Elton John's film producer husband David Furnish; actors Sadie Frost and Liz Hurley; and politician Simon Hughes.
The judgment comes two days after it was made public that Harry and his wife, Meghan Markle, are moving back to the U.K. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who are no longer working royals, decamped to California more than six years ago but will relocate back later this month to live in a nonroyal residence outside London.
Harry's defeat against Associated Newspapers brought an end to a trio of lawsuits accusing tabloid publishers of using unlawful tactics, such as phone hacking or hiring private detectives to dig up dirt on his life.
Harry won a judgment in 2023 that condemned the publishers of the Daily Mirror for “widespread and habitual” phone hacking. Last year, Rupert Murdoch’s flagship U.K. tabloid, The Sun, made an unprecedented apology for intruding on his life for years and agreed to pay substantial damages to settle his privacy invasion lawsuit.
Harry has said his litigation — in which he broke with royal family tradition to seek relief in the courts — was a primary source of his falling out with his father, King Charles III, and brother Prince William.
His grudge with the tabloids runs deep and his legal actions are part of his larger quest to reform the news media that he says damaged his relationships and made him “ paranoid beyond belief.”
He blames the press for the death of his mother, Princess Diana, who was killed in a car crash in 1997 while being pursued by paparazzi in Paris, and for attacks on his wife, Meghan, that led the couple to abandon royal life and move to the United States in 2020.

Stray dog menace forces 4-day closure of 10 schools in Chamoli's Narayanbagar
Ten schools in Chamoli's Narayanbagar area have been ordered to remain closed following a rise in incidents involving stray and aggressive dogs.
Ten schools in the Narayanbagar area of Chamoli district have been declared closed for students from August 20 to 23 following concerns over the growing menace of stray and aggressive dogs in the region.
The decision has been taken in the interest of student safety following a letter from the Pramukh, Kshetra Panchayat Narayanbagar, dated August 19, highlighting the threat posed by stray and aggressive dogs in the area.
The order was issued by Akash Saraswat, Chief Education Officer, Chamoli, in compliance with directions from the District Magistrate, Chamoli.
Under the order, students of the affected schools will remain on holiday during the four-day period, while teachers have been instructed to ensure that educational activities continue through online classes.

The Block Education Officer and Deputy Education Officer (Primary Education), Narayanbagar, have been directed to ensure compliance with the order across the concerned institutions.

According to the official order, the decision was taken specifically in view of the "serious threat posed by stray/aggressive dogs" and to prevent any untoward incident involving students.
The development has also raised concerns among local residents, as children travelling to and from schools may be particularly vulnerable to attacks by stray animals.
Earlier, reports from the area indicated that several dog-bite incidents had been reported in Narayanbagar, prompting authorities to step up measures to deal with the problem. Multi-department teams have also been involved in efforts to identify and control aggressive stray dogs in the affected areas.
The administration's immediate priority is to ensure the safety of students while maintaining continuity in their education through online teaching.
Authorities are expected to assess the situation before the scheduled reopening of schools after August 23 and take further measures depending on the threat level in the area.

Police said it followed a two-month investigation into suspicious activities at the farm. Drugs and equipment worth around 600m rand ($37m; £27m) were seized as well as an undisclosed amount of cash.
A number big meth labs on remote farms have been discovered by South African police over the last two years - with several involving Mexican nationals.
In May, police arrested 11 people, including four Mexicans, after uncovering a suspected drug lab worth $6m on a remote farm north-west of Johannesburg.
In September last year, five Mexicans were arrested after police dismantled a crystal meth lab, with drugs worth $20m, on a farm in the east of the country.
In July 2024, three Mexicans were among those arrested at a remote farm in Limpopo province where a crystal meth lab and drugs worth $108m were uncovered.
- How Mexican drug cartels have outsourced meth labs to Nigeria 
  - Published29 July
The five Musina farm suspects will appear in court on Monday to face charges relating to the manufacture and possession of illicit drugs.
"The discovery has exposed an alleged sophisticated, industrial-scale operation believed to have been established for the manufacture of dangerous illicit substances destined for distribution," the police said in a statement.
South Africa is as one of the largest crystal meth consumer markets in the world, according to the 2022 Global State of Harm Reduction report.
The UN says its geography and "porous borders" also make it an ideal transit point for illicit drug.
South Africa is not the only African country where illicit laboratories have been found.
In May this year, Nigeria's drug enforcement agency said it had "dealt another crippling blow" and dismantled "a highly sophisticated, multi-million-dollar Nigerian-Mexican methamphetamine production syndicate".
The lab at the centre of an ongoing court case was discovered in a dense forested area of the West African nation.
Counter-narcotics officials at the US-Africa Command (Africom) recently told the BBC that since 2023 14 Mexican-operated laboratories had been raided on the continent - found in Kenya, Mozambique, Nigeria and South Africa.
Experts believe this indicates criminal cartels in Mexico are increasing using Africa, not just as a trafficking hub, but also as a production base.

Mumbai’s clinics, nursing homes, hospitals, maternity homes and diagnostic centres will face intensive inspections as the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) has launched a special drive to check compliance with health, safety and regulatory norms. Teams constituted by the civic health department will inspect clinical establishments across the city and take action against those found violating prescribed rules.
State Health Department Orders Special Inspection Drive Across Maharashtra
The campaign follows directions from the state Health Department for a special inspection drive covering clinical establishments across Maharashtra. The BMC teams will also inspect sonography centres and other healthcare facilities to assess patient safety, essential infrastructure and compliance with applicable laws.
According to the state Health Department’s circular, inspections will cover compliance with the Clinical Establishments-related regulations, PCPNDT Act, MTP Act, ART Act, Biomedical Waste Management Rules, fire safety norms and FDA regulations. Teams will also verify whether mandatory facilities and safety standards are being maintained.
Violating Establishments To Face Action Under Relevant Laws
Officials have been instructed to document violations and prepare reports in the prescribed format. Establishments found flouting norms will face action under the relevant laws.
The inspection teams will prepare daily progress reports detailing the number of establishments inspected, the number found violating various regulations and the observations recorded during inspections. The reports will have to be signed by the concerned officials and submitted daily to the Assistant Health Officer (Nursing Homes).
The Assistant Health Officer will forward the reports to the Executive Health Officer, who will subsequently submit them to the Deputy Director of the Directorate of Health Services.
According to a senior BMC officer, the drive would also help identify quacks and illegal nursing homes operating in Mumbai and its suburbs. “The inspections will provide accurate information about such establishments, making it easier for the civic administration to initiate action against them,” said the official.
The drive is aimed at strengthening regulatory oversight of private healthcare establishments and ensuring that patients receive treatment in facilities equipped with the required infrastructure and operating in accordance with statutory safety and healthcare norms.

Satish Ghadge alias Satish Maratha, a 34-year-old history-sheeter, was murdered in Surat’s Bhestan area on 5 August 2026. He was attacked by a group of assailants while travelling in a car. Police suspect the killing was linked to an old gang rivalry. Four adults and four juveniles have been detained or arrested in connection with the case, and police are investigating the alleged conspiracy behind the murder (here, here, and here).
In this context, a post featuring a screenshot from a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that Satish Maratha was murdered by Muslim youths in Surat. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: Satish Maratha was murdered by Muslim youths in Surat.
Fact: None of the accused in the case are Muslims. S.B. Desai, in-charge of Surat’s Bhestan Police Station, told Factly that all the accused are Hindus and that the murder of Satish Ghadge alias Satish Maratha was the result of a personal rivalry. Police arrested nine accused, including four minors, in connection with the case. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A Google Lens search for the viral screenshot led us to multiple media reports (here, here, and here) published in August 2026 that featured the same visuals. According to these reports, 39-year-old Satish Maratha was brutally murdered on the afternoon of 5 August 2026 in the Bhestan area of Surat. Satish was travelling in his Swift car with a young woman when bike-borne assailants broke the car window. When he stepped out, the attackers surrounded him and assaulted him with swords and knives, reportedly inflicting more than 39 injuries. Police arrested nine accused in connection with the case, including four minors.
The reports also stated that Satish had a long-standing dispute with Rahul Mandal over a liquor stand and dominance in the area. Around a month and a half before the murder, Satish was reportedly attacked with chilli powder under the Godhra Bridge but survived. However, none of the reports mentions any involvement of Muslims in the incident.
To verify whether there was any communal angle to the incident, we contacted S.B. Desai, the in-charge of Surat’s Bhestan Police Station. He told Factly that all the accused in the Satish Maratha murder case are Hindus. He also stated that the murder was the result of a personal rivalry and confirmed that the three minors involved in the incident are also Hindus.
To sum up, none of the accused in the Satish Maratha murder case in Surat are Muslims.

On a recent afternoon in Washington, I put on a pair of augmented-reality glasses for a tour of some very recent ruins: the White House East Wing. In recent months, black fencing has overtaken the area, where Donald Trump’s ballroom construction is speeding along as the Supreme Court decides its fate. Visitors can’t see much of anything from the street. As I wore the clunky eyewear, though, historic images of the structure flashed in front of me. The glasses showed me features wiped away by the president during his ongoing renovation spree, such as the Jacqueline Kennedy Garden and the White House Family Theater. Looking around, I could see a panorama of images visualizing Trump’s plans to transform Washington, D.C.: the Reflecting Pool, the Triumphal Arch, the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, and more.
The tour guide, a public historian named Lexi Cleveland, created this very 2026 experience as the executive vice president of ARtGlass, an AR company. (One of the co-founders is Greg Werkheiser, a cultural-heritage lawyer currently suing the Trump administration over plans to paint the Eisenhower Executive Office Building.) Cleveland prompted me with questions throughout. “What do we actually lose when we lose a building?” she asked. When the glasses showed me a Black Lives Matter mural that the city removed after Trump’s return to office, Cleveland juxtaposed it with the equestrian statue of President Andrew Jackson in front of the White House. The populist Jackson is one of Trump’s favorite presidents; expanding slavery and signing the Indian Removal Act are inextricable parts of his legacy. The construction of the statue, completed in 1852, involved an enslaved apprentice. “If you got to decide,” Cleveland asked, “does the statue stay, go, get contextualized with signage, or get moved to a museum?”
She plans to ask these questions to larger groups when the tours start in full this month, and she’s prepared to mediate debates. The approach feels fitting in a country engaged in an active struggle over how to remember its past.
History is on Trump’s mind. He wants to become part of it by reshaping the commemorative landscape of Washington. And he wants to reframe how history is told within Washington’s museums. For over a year, the White House has scolded and threatened the Smithsonian. But last month, the president took an unprecedented step toward pushing that feud into the real world. In an executive order, he called on the National Park Service to place signs outside the National Museum of American History, which the White House has said is subject to “ideological capture” at the hands of “a radical activist cohort.” The Park Service will direct visitors to “accurate information” about the nation’s past and mount its own temporary exhibit about the signatories of the Declaration of Independence, who the White House says aren’t showcased enough by the museum. The fight for public memory will soon spill into the streets.
It will happen on the National Mall, where the National Guard continues to roam and not far from the transformed White House, with its abundant fencing—at this point, a core aesthetic of the second Trump administration. Across town, scaffolding outside the Kennedy Center blocks the part of the facade where Trump’s name once hung above the late president’s. Historic statues at Arlington Memorial Bridge have been swallowed up by blinding gold. Meanwhile, at two plazas in downtown Washington, statues that came down during the Black Lives Matter protests have been reinstalled: One of Confederate General Albert Pike returned to Judiciary Square last fall, and one of Caesar Rodney (which was toppled in Wilmington, Delaware), who signed the Declaration of Independence and enslaved hundreds of people, now overlooks Freedom Plaza.
Historians, preservationists, and activists are finding ways to work their own ideas and stories back into public space, in spite of the obstacles. The most visible example might be a series of viral art pieces by the guerilla art group the Secret Handshake that keep appearing on the Mall. (In March, the group plopped a gold toilet by the Lincoln Memorial to poke fun at Trump’s redevelopment projects.) But there are more sober ventures too. When Trump’s exhibit goes up outside the American History Museum, a group called Citizen Historians for the Smithsonian plans to send docents to “interpret” the signage for visitors—a nerdy form of counter-protest. Even the Smithsonian American Women’s History Museum, which has not yet been assigned a site because of partisan fighting in Congress, is oddly of a piece with this renegade spirit: It has resorted to an augmented-reality exhibit that dreams up some new monuments for D.C.
The projects get at the central disagreement fueling these feuds over history: whether, as Trump sees it, American history is best told through a simple, sweeping narrative of grandeur or, as these groups see it, through a compendium of diverse stories. If the city suddenly feels like it’s in rough-draft form, Trump isn’t the only one with a red pen in hand.
A few days after Trump issued his executive order about the National Museum of American History, I arrived at a very wholesome protest: about a dozen concerned museumgoers holding signs outside the staff entrance to the building and singing patriotic songs such as “My Country, ’Tis of Thee.” The makeshift choir is part of a larger group, Citizen Historians for the Smithsonian, that came together last year to archive material across the Smithsonian because it feared that the Trump administration might start altering exhibits. I found one of Citizen Historians’ leaders, Jessica Dickinson Goodman, explaining the recent drama to a group of tourists, a kind of test run for conversations to come.
Earlier this month, the group’s role expanded from DIY archivists to rogue docents when it put out a call for help interpreting the signage that Trump is adding to the Mall. In its newsletter, the group described the effort as nonconfrontational and fact-based. Dozens of volunteers came forward. Dickinson Goodman told me that they’re creating instructions for the types of topics that might arise: “We’ll start showing up as soon as we hear of construction starting.”
One place where the grand, old-school version of history that the Trump administration seems to prefer prevails in the monuments and memorials on the National Mall. Here, the subject matter is clear, and the tone, though solemn, is usually celebratory.
The sole memorial dedicated to a named historical woman is for Eleanor Roosevelt, though the statue is incorporated into her husband’s larger commemorative site. For its 250th celebration, the Smithsonian American Women’s History Museum put out its augmented-reality exhibit, “Unhidden Heroines,” to highlight five women associated with five major monuments—and to underscore their absence from public art. It’s hard not to perceive an exhibition squished onto your phone screen as an indicator of where women’s history stands these days.
Still, it’s worth a “visit.” At the Jefferson Memorial, the geotagged exhibition focuses on Mary Katharine Goddard, who printed the first copy of the Declaration of Independence to list most of the signers. At the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial, Dorothy Height talks about how she helped organize the March on Washington but did not speak at it. At the end of each anecdote, a “monument” of sorts pops up next to whatever your camera is pointing at. The figures appear so large on the screen, they sometimes dwarf the actual monuments. “That was intentional, of course, because they were towering women in their own right,” Karri Nussle, the museum’s associate director for advancement and external affairs, told me.
It was fun. Well done too. But sitting there with my phone and my headphones and the make-believe monuments, I also felt kind of sad. Eventually, the augmented-reality glasses come off. The phone screen goes black. The volunteer docents go home. What’s left? At the Jefferson Memorial, after I put my phone down, sending a cartoonish Mary Katharine Goddard back into the digital ether, it was just me and the man cast in bronze.

On 31 July, “Umit” – which means hope in Kazakh – was released into a nature reserve on the edge of Lake Balkhash after more than a decade of careful planning to return the caspian tiger to the region. With this release, Kazakhstan became the first country to restore its tiger range after they had been thought extinct, with the last reliable sighting in the country recorded more than 70 years ago.
Umit – a wild-caught female tiger transported from the Russian far east – will be joined by more big cats in the coming years, with plans to establish a self-sustaining population of about 50. A wild-caught male flown from Russia is still being monitored by authorities and will be released when he is judged fit to survive alone. Two wild tiger cubs are also being reared on the reserve in special enclosures, with as little human contact as possible, and are likely to be released into the marshlands next year, to feast on boar, deer and kulans, a type of wild donkey.
“Today, we became witnesses of a truly historic event,” declared Yerlan Nysanbayev, Kazakhstan’s environment minister, after the release. “There is a lot of work ahead on monitoring tigers and forming a stable population, but today the first and very important step has been taken.”
The caspian tiger was considered extinct in the 1970s after decades of fur hunting, habitat destruction and eradication campaigns. Its range once spanned from eastern Turkey to north-west China, including Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iran and swathes of central Asia, mostly in forest highlands and along the edges of lakes and rivers, particularly in Tugai forests that were widely destroyed for agriculture.
It was officially declared extinct in 2003, but a scientific breakthrough just six years later laid the foundation for the recent release. DNA analysis of the tiger’s genetic history revealed that the caspian tiger and the amur tiger found in eastern Siberia were almost identical, with populations probably intermingling until the early 1900s before they were isolated by hunting. What became known as the caspian tiger spread west from Siberia and were separated from the amur tiger by a single letter of genetic code.
“For all intents and purposes, this is the return of the caspian tiger, only this time they flew instead of walking,” said Dale Miquelle, an authority on Siberian tigers who formerly headed the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Russia programme. “The idea of bringing back a subspecies of tigers that has disappeared is very exciting. This is as close as we’re going to get to that process.”
Today, it would be practically impossible for the caspian tiger to re-establish its former range. A 2017 feasibility study identified two places in the region with enough suitable habitat to re-establish populations, both in Kazakhstan. The most promising was thought to be Ile-Balkhash, where Umit was released, which the Kazakh government made a nature reserve in 2018.
While this summer’s release is the first example of a cross-border tiger translocation, there have been several successful releases in the Russian far east as part of efforts to restore the amur tiger’s former range. One scheme involved rescuing orphaned cubs whose mothers had been shot by hunters in Siberia, and then releasing them into former ranges when they were strong enough. The project, which Miquelle worked on, was a huge success – especially because there was no human contact with the young big cats.
“The success rate was pretty close to 100% after the release. These animals adapt amazingly quickly. One young female killed a Himalayan black bear within 24 hours of being released and others have learned to hunt on their own in the wild really quickly,” he says.
But it is not all good news. Wild tigers have suffered a catastrophic century, with numbers falling from about 100,000 at the beginning of the 20th century to about 5,500 today. In many parts of Asia, they are still declining – and facing new threats from climate breakdown and disease. In recent years in Russia, African swine fever wiped out enormous numbers of wild boar, a tiger’s favourite prey, causing many to target human settlements. Ensuring there is enough food for the returning caspian tigers is key to their survival, says Miquelle.
“I am very hopeful this can work. In Russia, a number of translocations resulted in the recolonisation of tiger habitat. So there’s a blueprint that suggests that this can work as long as there is suitable habitat and sufficient prey,” he says.

What will unite tennis and pickleball players? A whole lot more courts
Planners and sports policy experts say there aren't enough recreational facilities for any sport
Nearly anywhere you go in this country, tennis and pickleball players are locked in a fierce competition for court time.
When two public tennis courts in Scarborough, Ont., were converted into six pickleball courts late last year, for example, one local tennis player launched a petition calling on the city to reverse course.
On the more extreme end of things, a conflict between pickleball and tennis players over access to public courts on Mayne Island, B.C., went all the way to B.C.'s Supreme Court.
But these local squabbles are "just a microcosm of what's happening right across the landscape of sports and recreation," says Matti Siemiatycki, a professor of geography and planning at the University of Toronto. Also the director of the university's Infrastructure Institute, Siemiatycki says there are not enough public recreational facilities for any sport.
"Whether it's a hockey arena space, which is always at a premium, whether it's tennis space, whether it is park space, all of the swimming pool space — all of this is fiercely contested and how we're allocating it is both challenging and in some cases creating inequalities," he told CBC's The Sunday Magazine.
Experts in planning and sports policy say the answer is not to leave sports communities to duke it out over who has access to the publicly owned facilities, and nor is it to leave sport entirely in the hands of for-profit organizations and those who can afford to pay. The answer, they say, is to try to address the supply problem instead.
To that end, housing developers should have to build more recreational facilities than the current rules demand, says Peter Donnelly, a University of Toronto professor emeritus who directed the Centre for Sports Policy Studies before he retired.
"I'd love to see them get back to the same kind of public housing policies that were in place after the Second World War, where Canada built hundreds of thousands of homes across the country and did so, very often, with including parks and recreational space and community centres as a part of that development," Donnelly said.
"I think the developers just won the war on that."
Should developers do more?
Here's how things have typically worked until fairly recently.
Housing developers who wanted approval for a project that had, say, taller towers than the land was zoned for, had to enter into a negotiation with the municipality, which usually involved some level of community consultation as well, said Siemiatycki.
Planning legislation in the provinces and territories tended to give municipalities quite a bit of power to determine how much the developers would pay for things like recreational facilities, parkland dedication, daycare spaces and public art.
But in response to the housing crisis, these governments have started to reduce how much municipalities can charge developers, says Siemiatycki. That's because of concerns these charges were bogging down the process of getting houses built, and that developers were passing those costs on to new homeowners, elevating prices even more, he says.
In Ontario, changes that came into effect in September 2022 capped community benefits charges at four per cent of the appraised value of the land at the time the building permit is issued.
"What it means is that, in practice, there's going to be less money for some of these park and recreation spaces," said Siemiatycki.
Growth in pickleball and tennis
These changes happened while more people were picking up racket sports.
"There's been a huge explosion in interest in pickleball over the last number of years and really a recommitment to tennis since the pandemic," said Siemiatycki.
Both games fit the bill for sports you can play outdoors and in a socially-distanced fashion.
Though CBC is unable to verify their figures, both Tennis Canada and Pickleball Canada claim that participation has grown significantly in the last few years.
Jonathan Moody, president of Pickleball Ontario, says the game is ideally played on smaller courts with slightly lower nets. But in most cities, outdoor players usually "make do" on tennis courts, he says.
Public-private partnerships?
A host of pickleball businesses have sprouted up in response to demand. Amen Pickleball converted an empty church in the Montreal suburb of Chambly, Que., U.S. chain Pickler opened its first Canadian location in a Winnipeg business park in January. A company called Fairgrounds opened locations in several provinces, some in empty shopping mall spaces.
Lyndsay Hayhurst is an associate professor at York University's School of Kinesiology and Health Science in Toronto whose research interests include sport and gender, as well as how sports can contribute to community engagement and development.
Hayhurst said while there's been "a lot of excitement" about the privately-owned pickleball businesses, "when you look at who can actually afford it long term, it's not an equity denied individual who's living below the poverty line."
But Hayhurst says she sees potential for city recreation departments to partner with these businesses to offer some memberships for free, or to bring in youth from nearby schools.
The tax angle
Property taxes are one of the few mechanisms that municipalities have to raise funds for local facilities. But increasing property taxes can be a political hot potato for local governments.
Some places have tried a "sin tax" approach, says Siemiatycki. In the U.K., for example, a portion of lottery money is used for local infrastructure and facilities.
Unfortunately, he says, there's no magic funding model that's just waiting to be discovered.
When cities are trying to tangle with major problems like housing affordability, things like recreation space can slip down the priority list.
"Public spaces can often seem low stakes," said Siemiatycki, "but really how they're used and who has access can really shape how a community sees itself."
As sports policy expert Peter Donnelly puts it, parks and rec departments are "treated as kind of the toy department of most city councils and it's just become a huge problem."
Donnelly says it's time for cities to take recreation more seriously. "I go back to the bottom line on this. Active healthy communities are really good places to live."
