A team of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) was allegedly chased away by locals as they visited the Bagru Assembly constituency of Jaipur in Rajasthan on Friday, August 21. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke alleged that the outfit's co-convenor, Ashutosh Ranka, was "attacked by BJP goons" in Rajasthan. The incident took place when Ranka, accompanied by a CJP team, visited a government school in Rampura Kanwarpura village in Jaipur, which he claimed had been operating in a buffalo shed for the past several years. The CJP had launched “School Thik Karo” campaign on August 15. A confrontation broke out between the villagers and the CJP workers, including co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka, following which the latter were pushed out of the area, sources told PTI. "...some of our team members who had arrived there, BJP goons have once again resorted to violence against them," Ranka alleged. He said, "The BJP is fine with our children continuing to study in a buffalo shed, but if we try to get these schools fixed, that is not acceptable to them." He asked, “What could be more shameful than this?” The school building in the village was reportedly closed for students after being declared 'unsafe'. Classes are currently being held in a cattle enclosure near the school building. Sharing a few videos from the spot, Dipke questioned the Rajasthan police on Friday as locals allegedly pushed a CJP team out of a village where it had gone to inspect a government school. "Ashu and other volunteers of CJP were beaten up and have been injured," Dipke claimed. "@PoliceRajasthan seems to be a mute spectator while goons attack CJP volunteers for visiting govt schools. They don’t seem to have a problem with schools running in buffalo stables, but somehow have a problem with CJP volunteers entering those schools. What exactly are they trying to protecting," Dipke posted on X. Videos shared by Dipke on social media and other leaders showed a mob chasing away CJP team members. Another image showed a car's broken windshield. "@PoliceRajasthan has allowed this to happen," Dipke said while continuing his attack on the Rajasthan police. "Goons of BJP are after the blood of Ashutosh and other CJP volunteers. How can @PoliceRajasthan allow this kind of attack?," Dipke wrote in another post on X, as he shared a video showing locals stopping the team of CJP from proceeding. Attacking the BJP in another X post, Dipke wrote, "[The] BJP wants your children to study in a buffalo shed. Ashu wants them to study in a better school. That’s why they attacked him today when he was going to expose the buffalo-shed school." The CJP team had planned to visit two government schools in Jaipur on Friday to assess their infrastructure and the facilities available to the students. Friday's visit followed a controversy over the entry of the public and media into government schools in Rajasthan. Following earlier inspections by the CJP, the state education department reportedly restricted the entry of outsiders and mediapersons into schools without a specific reason. Congress MLA Sachin Pilot said, "State Govt has issued a fresh order that no journalist can enter a school, no photos can be taken, and nothing can be reported. They want to keep their failures hidden. The bad condition of schools - dilapidated buildings and children have died. The situation is very serious. Instead of taking remedial measures, Govt is issuing such orders. They will have to withdraw this order. This is not the right direction for our democracy..." Trump can keep building his White House ballroom, for now, Supreme Court rules
Construction can continue on the president’s sprawling ‘military complex’ and heavily fortified ballroom while a legal battle plays out
The Supreme Court will let Donald Trump continue building his White House ballroom and “military complex” while a legal challenge against the East Wing’s demolition and sprawling construction project continues.
Friday’s one-page decision from Chief Justice John Roberts gives the president permission to keep building what his administration is increasingly describing as a highly fortified military installation that is vital to the safety and security of the president.
A months-long legal battle has stalled construction, but the president urged the Supreme Court last week to intervene and let him build what he has called a “desperately needed National Security structure” — including a massive underground bunker and rooftop military complex with a bulletproof, hermetically sealed ballroom built with nuclear-blast-resistant materials sandwiched in between.
On August 7, a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. ordered the government to stop construction on the project by Friday unless Congress — or the Supreme Court — stepped in.
With Friday’s order, the administration can continue construction while the Supreme Court considers its next steps. The justices and federal court judges will likely hear more arguments over the plans and whether Trump subverted the role of Congress with his unilateral decision to demolish the East Wing.
Trump’s plans initially envisioned an ornate White House ballroom stuffed with gold finishes and marble floors, but court filings over the last several months have detailed what officials called “top secret” designs that revealed the primary purpose of the 90,000-square-foot ballroom project.
The president told reporters at the White House on Monday that military officials approached him with plans for the military complex after he announced his intentions to build a ballroom last year.
He said he was told there is an “opportunity to build deep into the ground and build a military facility to go with the White House — and to go with all of Washington, D.C., which would be so valuable.”
The ballroom is “a knitted, unified, cohesive part of the East Wing Project, which is vital for National Security, and is being constructed to ensure that the President can perform his constitutional duties in a safe and heavily secured facility,” government lawyers wrote in court documents this summer.
The project will include“heavy steel, drone-proof roof, missile-resistant and drone-proof columns, bullet, ballistic, and blast-proof glass, Military-grade venting for air conditioning and heating” as well as “bomb shelters, a state of the art hospital and medical facilities, Top Secret military installations, structures, and equipment, protective partitioning, and other features,” according to the Department of Justice.
If the Supreme Court didn’t halt construction, the project “will in all likelihood become irreversible,” preservationists who sued the administration wrote to the justices this week.
Because the construction materials are meant to withstand even nuclear blasts, there would be no way to take any of it down even if the courts intervened later, the group argued.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation said the administration’s “striking admission” that the project is “on the brink of a fait accompli” is precisely why the Supreme Court must stop construction now.
“The question is simply who decides whether a ballroom can be built on federal property. Our constitutional system and federal law commits that choice to Congress,” the group wrote.
There is nothing that prevents the president from asking Congress for one — “today, tomorrow, or any time in the future,” they added.
But Trump’s attempt to “foil judicial review and arrogate Congress’s exclusive powers should not be rewarded” with a court order that allows him to continue construction that he lacked “any authority to commence in the first place,” the group argued.
Federal courts have now repeatedly blocked parts of the project from moving forward without approval from Congress, but Democratic and Republican leaders don’t seem interested in getting involved.
“We don’t believe we have to go to Congress. We believe Congress has already given us the authority to do what we’re doing,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said during an appearance on Fox News Sunday. “Many presidents have done a tremendous amount of work to the White House, as they should, and Congress has authorized them to do so.”
Costs for the project have exploded from an initial $200 million estimate to $400 million — with some believing it could cost upwards of $600 million.
While Trump has said private donations will pay for the ballroom itself, the administration transferred more than $300 million from the Secret Service budget to cover security upgrades to the White House this summer.

New Delih: Cities are staring at an ₹11.5 trillion capital expenditure requirement between FY27 and FY31, but most of them are in no shape to borrow for it. Only 223 of the country's 4,332 urban local bodies (ULBs) currently have credit-rating reports, a gap that keeps the vast majority of municipalities locked out of market-based financing, even as an indicative ₹5.8 trillion credit opportunity exists over the same period. The mismatch was among the central issues discussed at the two-day Public Sector Banks (PSB) Conclave 2026, held earlier this week in the national capital in the presence of Union finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman, according to people aware of the discussions and a document reviewed by Mint. The stakes are high. India's urban population is expected to cross 53% of the total by FY2047, and cities are projected to generate nearly 70% of GDP by then. Around 70% of the urban infrastructure needed to support that growth, spanning housing, metro rail, roads, water supply, waste management and logistics, is yet to be built. To close the gap, the framework under discussion envisages a bigger role for public financial institutions (PFIs) in helping municipalities become more creditworthy. The idea is to link credit access to improvements in how municipalities collect property tax and user charges, and to how they modernise revenue systems more broadly, one person aware of the discussions said. The plan also includes standardising financial reporting across municipalities and building common frameworks for municipal credit assessment, so that rating exercises can happen more regularly. That's a big ask: roughly half of ULB revenue currently comes from taxes and fees, with the rest made up of grants and investment income, leaving many municipalities financially dependent on higher levels of government. Separately, the National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development (NaBFID) said it could step in with partial credit enhancement (PCE), essentially, a guarantee that improves a project's credit profile, for eligible municipal projects. “PCE is closely linked to credit ratings and is equally applicable to municipal projects. From NaBFID's perspective, PCE may be extended to eligible municipal projects to enhance their credit rating profile, thereby improving bankability and facilitating access to institutional and market-based financing,” a NaBFID spokesperson said in an emailed response. The spokesperson added that one of the biggest hurdles municipalities face is the absence of solid financial management, bookkeeping and accounting practices. Government schemes such as the Urban Challenge Fund (UCF) are meant to push municipal corporations toward better financial discipline and stronger cash-flow management, particularly for projects run as public-private partnerships, the spokesperson said. Emailed queries to the finance and housing ministries, and to India Infrastructure Finance Co. Ltd, went unanswered as of press time. The municipal bond market itself remains tiny, despite a revival in recent years. As of 31 July 2026, ULBs had raised a total of ₹4,540.34 crore through 31 municipal bond issuances by around 22 ULBs, according to SEBI data. The current phase of the market picked up after 2017, helped by incentives under the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT and AMRUT 2.0), along with better credit ratings and regulatory support. Most recent issuances have carried investment-grade ratings, typically AA or AA+, with maturities of five to 10 years and coupons broadly between 7.6% and 8.5%. The money raised has largely gone into water supply, sewerage, roads, and green infrastructure projects. Before 2017, issuances were limited and dated back to the late 1990s. Including those older bonds and special cases like the ₹2,000 crore Amaravati Bonds issued by the Andhra Pradesh Capital Region Development Authority, the cumulative market size is estimated at roughly ₹6,000-6,100 crore. The Amaravati bond is sometimes included in the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs' broader tallies, but it doesn't figure in the Securities and Exchange Board of India's dedicated ULB bond statistics. Even after the post-2017 revival, the market remains shallow by global standards: India's municipal bond market is equivalent to just 0.06% of its corporate bond market, compared with 7% in the US. Officials pointed to two structural problems. First, project cash flows aren't adequately ring-fenced, meaning revenue from a specific project isn't clearly separated to guarantee repayment. Project-finance structures and escrow mechanisms for project revenues could offer investors more certainty on debt servicing, one of the people said. Second, weak disclosure and small, fragmented project pipelines make it hard to attract long-term institutional money. Pooling smaller projects into larger financing vehicles — potentially through state-level intermediaries or dedicated municipal infrastructure funds — could help create bigger, more investable portfolios. “The experience of Surat shows how greater participation of urban local bodies in the municipal bond market can directly translate into better urban infrastructure and public amenities,” Hemali Boghawala, former mayor of Surat Municipal Corporation. Surat's green bond proceeds are funding water treatment, renewable energy, waste processing and electric buses, showing how market financing can reduce cities' dependence on government grants, she added. The broader framework aims to attract a broader base of institutional investors to municipal bonds through mechanisms such as expanded credit enhancement, underwriting of anchor tranches, and partial guarantees. “For India's urban infrastructure financing needs, the longer-term opportunity will therefore depend not only on the quantum of capital available but also on whether municipalities can strengthen their own-source revenues, improve financial disclosures, ring-fence project cash flows and build sufficient creditworthiness to access debt markets,” said a senior government official, requesting anonymity. Taking a safe bet here that most of you who have heard of Louise Joy Brown have not heard at all of Jean Purdy, or her role in the birth of Baby Brown. Louise Brown was the first baby born of an IVF procedure on July 25, 1978. But this might not have been a joyful story, but for Jean Purdy.
Like all the heroines in this column, Jean Marian Purdy, a clinical embryologist and a critical part of the development of in vitro fertilisation, remained uncredited for a long while. Born in Cambridge, U.K., she went to work with physiologist Robert Edwards and gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe at the Physiological Laboratory in Cambridge. They were working on a high-risk experiment and taking medical science where it had never been before – who would have thought babies could be created in test tubes before the trio managed to show that it is possible.
Purdy trained as a nurse in Addenbrooke Hopsital in Cambridge, and joined Edwards in 1968 as a research nurse and quickly became indispensable to the team. Going back to study the records later, scientists established that it was Purdy who managed the laboratory, prepared and tested culture media, and recorded and organised the data of the early IVF work in the lab. Besides this, the records also put her at the centre of patient care, in this case, supporting women who volunteered their eggs and wombs at a time when public sentiment was entirely against it.
Purdy was the first to recognise and describe the formation of the early human blastocyst – the cluster of cells that forms five or six days after a sperm fertilises an egg, in the culture, a key milestone in pre-implantation development. It represents the early stage of embryonic development, where the embryo implants itself into the wall of the uterus to establish a pregnancy. Purdy was the first to see the embryonic cells successfully dividing in the lab, soon these cells would go on to become on 25 July 1978, she was the first to see the embryonic cells that would become Louise Brown. This moment is significant, because it was the first indication that their pioneering technique had worked.
That was not all; between 1970 and 1985, until her death, she co-authored 26 academic papers with Edwards and others in leading journals, including Nature, documenting methods, outcomes and sophistication that made IVF safe and more reliable.
After NHS funding for IVF was withdrawn following early successes, Purdy helped establish the world’s first dedicated IVF clinic, Bourn Hall Clinic near Cambridge in 1980, and served as its technical director. Again, she helped standardise medical protocols for IVF and scale up treatment, overseeing the birth of more than 500 IVF babies before her death from cancer at just 39 years, in 1985.
In their article The Oldham Notebooks: an analysis of the development of IVF 1969–1978. V. The role of Jean Purdy reassessed, archived in PubMed, Martin H. Johnson and Kay Elder, look at her body of work in early fertility care. The authors pored over the Oldham Notebooks - 21 handwritten laboratory notebooks and loose records kept primarily by Purdy between 1969 and 1978. They concluded that: “Purdy’s interests were clearly focused on the research and development aspects, especially those exploring viable embryo development and improved transfer procedures. For example, in a film made in 1980 (Williams, 1980), she talks about a modification to the transfer cannula that she was trying. Thus, whilst Edwards provided the ideas and the intellectual stimulation and Steptoe the authoritative clinical skills, it is arguable that without Purdy’s systematic approach and dedicated contributions, the project at Oldham may have faltered.”
Despite all this, centuries of sexism weighing in on the scientific community, a classic example of the Matilda Effect, her role was minimised in public memory for decades. Even though Edwards and other colleagues objected to it, Purdy’s name was omitted from a commemorative plaque installed at Oldham Hopsitals, associated with IVF’s breakthrough. Correspondence from Edwards archived at Cambridge later described Purdy as “crucial” to their work, underscoring how her erasure contradicted the team’s own view of her importance. In fact, Edwards’ own records state his growing confidence in her and her essentiality in the team: Purdy was “being ‘particularly good with the patients’, and her ‘cooperation had become crucial. It was no longer just Patrick and me. We had become a threesome’.
However, only Edwards was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for IVF. While recognition for the work that Purdy did, has grown only recently, thanks in good measure to the research of Johnson and Elder, some things cannot be corrected any more. Now, some museums and clinics cite Purdy as the first clinical embryologist, and other institutions have begun naming awards and exhibitions after her. Sidelined again, this time, though her collaborators acknowledged her work, Purdy’s contributions were callously and credit consistently denied.
Though belated, it’s now time to undo the wrongs. It is time to say her name! Say Jean Purdy, shout it out from the rooftops!

Can Microdramas Turn Minutes Into Money? India’s microdrama space is turning into a serious battlefield. Short vertical stories are winning audiences across languages and smaller cities, while emerging and established players are battling rising acquisition costs. So, what exactly is cooking in India’s microdrama arena? A Desi Format Emerges: Microdramas may have originated in China, but India is developing its own version of the format. Platforms are adapting stories, pacing and characters to local languages, formats and cultural contexts. Not just this, a majority of viewers are from tier II+ cities, with many preferring native-language content and stories rooted in everyday life. The Cost Conundrum: Microdrama production is relatively inexpensive, with a series costing around ₹10-15 Lakh. But the real expense begins afterwards. Rising customer acquisition costs are making it difficult for platforms to acquire viewers, keep them engaged and convert them into paying users. Then, there are the distribution challenges for specialist players such as Kuku TV and Story TV, which have to figure out a way to find users. While monetisation remains the big challenge, advertising could become a stronger revenue stream. But brands are still treating microdramas as an experimental channel. Big Guns On The Prowl: JioHotstar, Zee Entertainment, Tata Play and Amazon MX Player have all launched short-format offerings. Their entry could threaten standalone startups by intensifying competition for talent, users and content, but it may also help establish microdramas as a mainstream category. From Content To IP: The next phase will require platforms to build memorable intellectual property rather than simply produce large volumes of low-cost content. Industry executives believe that the winners will combine differentiated stories, large-scale distribution and strong technology. Localisation will also be important, while AI could also reduce production timelines and operating costs without replacing creative teams. So, can microdrama platforms convert high watch time and cultural relevance into repeatable revenue? Much of this is burned, worsening air pollution and releasing carbon. LongStraw Carbon is trying to flip this equation by turning waste into biochar and bio-oil. From Residue To Carbon: Founded in 2024, LongStraw Carbon uses pyrolysis to convert agricultural waste into biochar, bio-oil and syngas. By heating biomass in the absence of oxygen, the startup transforms crop residue into products that can replace wasteful burning while retaining carbon in a stable form. In Odisha, its projects source rice husk and other residues from nearby mills, then process the material into biochar and related outputs. The startup also claims that this approach can improve soil health, reduce dependence on fertilisers and create local employment. Commercialising Carbon: The startup sells biochar to farmers and industrial customers, while generating additional revenue from bio-oil. Its model also connects to voluntary carbon markets, where companies are seeking independently assessed removal credits to support net-zero commitments. Scaling The Platform: LongStraw is targeting 1 Lakh tonnes of biochar production annually by 2028. The company is building around rice-mill partnerships and a circular “Riceloop” model that connects feedstock, energy, soil applications and carbon finance. New Delhi, Aug 21: Union Minister for Health and Family Welfare, J P Nadda, today reviewed the prevailing situation and preparedness for H1N1 Influenza in the country, with particular focus on the National Capital. Delhi Health Minister Dr. Pankaj Kumar Singh also attended the meeting.
The Union Health Minister reviewed the national surveillance and epidemiological situation, Influenza-like illness (ILI) and Severe Acute Respiratory Infection (SARI) trends, testing and laboratory surveillance, and preparedness of healthcare facilities to manage seasonal influenza cases. Nadda emphasised the need for continued vigilance, robust surveillance and proactive preparedness, with close monitoring of influenza trends and timely identification and management of any unusual increase or clustering of cases.
The preparedness of healthcare facilities in Delhi was reviewed, including the availability of hospital beds, critical care facilities, oxygen-supported beds, ventilators, essential medicines, diagnostics, and other critical supplies. The Minister stressed the importance of adequate surge capacity and seamless referral mechanisms, particularly for patients requiring specialised or critical care.
The Union Health Minister called for continued strengthening of early detection, timely testing and appropriate clinical management of influenza cases, along with effective utilisation of the existing surveillance and laboratory network.
Earlier, on 10th July 2026, the Union Health Secretary had written to all States/UTs advising them to strengthen preparedness and surveillance for Acute Respiratory Illness (ARI) and ensure healthcare facilities remain adequately prepared.
Nadda also emphasised public awareness and preventive health practices, including respiratory hygiene and hand hygiene, and advised individuals with persistent or severe respiratory symptoms, breathing difficulty or other warning signs to seek medical advice promptly.
The Union Health Minister reiterated that the situation is being closely and continuously monitored, while emphasising the need for sustained and coordinated efforts for the prevention and control of seasonal diseases, including Dengue and Malaria. Nadda called for a proactive and preparedness-oriented approach by State Governments, with active participation of Municipal Councillors and other local bodies in generating awareness among communities on the prevention, spread and control of seasonal diseases.
Highlighting the increase in TB detection in the National Capital through the active involvement of local bodies and a whole-of-government approach, the Union Minister stressed the importance of active participation of public representatives at all levels in disseminating factual and evidence-based information and strengthening community engagement.
The Ministry continues to coordinate closely with States/UTs, hospitals, laboratories and other stakeholders to ensure effective surveillance, early detection, timely clinical management and proactive preparedness for seasonal influenza, including H1N1.
The meeting was also attended by Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava; Additional Secretary (Public Health) Dr. Rakesh Gupta; Delhi State Health Secretary Rupesh Kumar Thakur and other senior officers.

Many soft-tissue sarcomas, which are rare types of cancers that form in fat, muscles and blood vessels, initially look like ordinary lumps. However, when a suspicious mass of this sort is removed without appropriate imaging, tissue diagnosis or oncological planning, the opportunity for the simplest and best-planned first operation may already have been lost.
Sarcomas in India, are therefore not only a problem of late diagnosis. Some are also operated on before a diagnosis is properly established. A first operation performed without sarcoma-specific planning can make subsequent treatment more extensive, even when the disease remains potentially curable.
A retrospective analysis in AIIMS, Delhi of 157 patients with localised extremity synovial sarcoma found that more than 70% of patients reached a specialist centre only after an unplanned surgery or a recurrence.
It may not look serious
Sarcomas are rare, accounting for about 1% of cancers in adults and roughly 15% of cancers in children. Their rarity is part of the challenge. Most soft-tissue lumps are benign, so neither patients nor clinicians naturally assume that a new lump is a cancer. Yet sarcoma can present with little more than a slowly enlarging swelling.
A soft-tissue sarcoma may appear well circumscribed, but that apparent boundary can be deceptive. Some tumours develop a surrounding pseudocapsule, and microscopic tumour cells may extend into or beyond it. If a sarcoma is removed without appropriate oncological margins, residual tumour may remain in the surgical bed. The operation that follows may then need to remove the previous scar and potentially contaminated tissues and, in some patients, may require more complex reconstruction.
Why unplanned removals are risky
The term ‘unplanned excision’ is used when a soft-tissue sarcoma is removed without appropriate preoperative imaging, histological confirmation or an oncological surgical plan. Evidence does not support the idea that such an operation automatically destroys the chance of cure. However, it can increase the risk of local recurrence and frequently creates the need for a second, wider operation to clear the tumour bed.
The AIIMS synovial sarcoma series illustrates both sides of this problem. Despite more than 70% of patients arriving after an unplanned operation or recurrence, limb salvage was still achieved in 64%. This is an important message for patients: an earlier inappropriate operation is serious, but it does not mean that amputation or treatment failure is inevitable. Prompt referral to a sarcoma team can still preserve meaningful treatment options.
Signs that should trigger a referral
Not every lump needs an MRI or a biopsy. But certain features should make a clinician stop before simply removing it. A soft-tissue mass that is enlarging, is about 5 centimetres or larger, lies deep to the fascia, has suspicious or indeterminate imaging features, or has returned after a previous removal deserves specialist assessment. Current imaging guidance recommends referral to a sarcoma or tumour reference centre before biopsy or surgery, when sarcoma is suspected.
For a suspicious extremity soft-tissue mass, MRI is usually the preferred local imaging test. If malignancy remains a concern, a carefully planned image-guided core-needle biopsy is generally the standard way to establish the diagnosis before definitive surgery. Small, superficial lesions may sometimes be managed differently, which is why the decision should be based on the whole clinical and imaging picture, rather than size alone.
Pain is not a reliable safety signal. Soft-tissue sarcoma can present as a painless lump, and the absence of pain should not reassure someone if a mass is enlarging or has other concerning features. The practical message is simple: a persistent or growing unexplained lump deserves an assessment, not an assumption.
Multi-disciplinary care
Sarcoma is not one disease but a heterogeneous family of cancers with many distinct subtypes. Diagnosis and treatment may require input from musculoskeletal radiology, specialist pathology, surgical oncology or orthopaedic oncology, radiation oncology and medical oncology. This is why major guidelines emphasise assessment in, or in close collaboration with, a specialist sarcoma centre when the diagnosis is suspected.
Image-guided core-needle biopsy has high diagnostic accuracy when it is properly planned and interpreted by experienced teams. The concern that a needle biopsy will routinely ‘spread’ a sarcoma is also misleading. Tumour seeding along a percutaneous biopsy tract is possible, but published data suggest that it is uncommon. The biopsy route should still be planned carefully because the tract may need to be considered during definitive surgery.
Dispelling harmful beliefs
Three beliefs are particularly harmful: that a painless lump must be harmless, that biopsy itself is more dangerous than obtaining a diagnosis, and that sarcoma automatically means amputation. None is a safe assumption. Modern sarcoma care is built around diagnosis before definitive treatment and, for extremity tumours, limb-preserving treatment is possible for many patients.
Better referral pathways between primary care, general surgical services and specialist centres can prevent avoidable unplanned excisions. The goal is not to send every small lump to a cancer centre; it is to recognise the few features that should trigger imaging, biopsy planning and specialist input before the first incision.
The first operation on a suspected sarcoma can shape what becomes necessary afterwards. For an unexplained lump with concerning features, diagnosis and planning should come before excision. Sometimes the most important cancer treatment decision is the one made before anyone enters the operating theatre.
(Dr. Siddharth Turkar is a consultant in medical oncology at Apollo Hospitals Navi Mumbai. drsiddharth_t@apollohospitals.com)

HyperX's first open-back gaming headset brings the bass
The Cloud Alpha Air is reasonably priced at $150 and sports super comfy earpads.
HyperX has been making gaming accessories for over a decade (and well before that if you count stuff like RAM and SSDs), but somehow in all that time, the company has never made an open-back gaming headset. But that changes today with the $150 Cloud Alpha Air, which comes with plush foam earpads and a Bass Tube designed to preserve that low-end thump.
One of the issues for open-back headphones is that when compared to closed-backed rivals, there's often a bit of bass loss due their more airy soundstage. However, on the Cloud Alpha Air, HyperX wanted to deliver the same low-end response you get from closed-back cans to help gamers more easily pick up on sound effects like footsteps and explosions. And during my short hands-on time with the Cloud Alpha Air so far, they certainly deliver.
HyperX's cans produce a really satisfying and controlled deep rumble that gave me a newfound appreciation for Nintendo's Wii Shop Channel theme without overpowering the mids and highs. And in games, its bass response highlighted low tones in shooters, though I don't know if it's enough to really give anyone a significant competitive advantage over similarly priced rivals. The Cloud Air Alpha also have an impedance of 34 ohms, which is relatively low, though I noticed that when I connected them to my PC via 3.5mm audio cable, overall volume was a tiny bit subdued, so discerning audiophiles may want to opt for HyperX's included USB adapter or rely on their own DAC. And just like you'd expect, you can tweak the Cloud Alpha Air's EQ and sound profile inside HyperX's free NGENUITY app.
As for the rest of the Cloud Alpha Air's design, HyperX kept things really simple. The only controls on the headphones themselves are a volume wheel and a mute button for its detachable mic. The sides of the cans feature a metallic grille that hides its red 40mm dynamic drivers underneath, while big foam earcups covered in ultrasuede provide a very comfy relaxed fit that makes them extremely easy to wear for long periods of time. Meanwhile, the metal headband feels quite sturdy and it easily withstood my bend test that consists of not-so-gently torquing each cup in opposite directions.
However, my favorite detail about the Cloud Alpha Air is that they come with full complement of cables and adapters including a basic 3.5mm cord, a PC extension cable with separate audio and mic jacks and a USB adapter that comes with both USB-A and USB-C connectors, so you can plug the headphones into pretty much any gadget you can think of. And to round out the kit, you even get a drawstring bag to pack everything into while traveling.
All told, it's a pretty nice package, especially considering that it's relatively affordable at $150. The only downside is that the Cloud Alpha Air is currently only available as a wired set of headphones. When I'm at home and battery life isn't really an issue, I like having the freedom to get up and walk around while chatting on Discord or listening to music without worrying about cables getting all tangled up. But alas, that's not an option quite yet. I strongly suspect that HyperX is working on a wireless version sometime in the future, but when I asked a company rep directly, they declined to comment. That said, the Cloud Alpha Air isn't the only pair of headphones HyperX is launching today, as the company is releasing new color combos for existing products including the HyperX Cloud III S, HyperX Cloud III Wired and HyperX Cloud Flight 2.
Alternatively, for those looking for new input options, HyperX created its lightest mouse yet in the Pulsefire Haste 3 Pro ($130). Made out of a carbon fiber shell and weighing just 47 grams, if you didn't know better, you'd think the mouse was empty inside. That said, it features the company's new Performance Sensor which delivers up to 42,000 DPI while still providing up to 150 hours of use (at 1K polling) in wireless mode. And if $130 feels a bit steep, HyperX also made a more affordable Pro Model for $90 featuring the same sensor and general features but with a slightly heavier plastic shell. Finally, if that's still too much, there's an even more budget-friendly wired model available for just $40.
Unfortunately, if you're in the market for a new PC, aside from some updated AMD-based configs for the Omen 35L, it seems HyperX is waiting a bit longer to announce any new gaming laptops or desktops. But for those looking to upgrade their rig with some fresh peripherals while waiting for the price of RAM to come down, HyperX has a bunch of reasonably-priced accessories to consider this fall when these devices go on sale sometime in September.

The Premier League's new plan to end corner chaos
- Published
Holding, pushing, shoving, jostling and grappling inside the penalty area became something of an epidemic in the Premier League last season.
"You get the feeling now that referees really don't want to get involved in any of it," Everton boss David Moyes said after a particularly fractious game against Manchester United in February.
"It's really poor that they've not tried to deal with it."
Then came West Ham's disallowed goal against Arsenal in May, when up to five potential fouls happened at the same time.
It was one of the key topics when captains, coaches, referees and other stakeholders were consulted in the summer.
So now, try to deal with it they will.
The Premier League season will get under way on Friday night when champions Arsenal host promoted Coventry, with referees instructed to be stronger, stricter and more ready to penalise clear non-footballing actions.
What does this mean? Will it be successful? And are the players and coaches on board too?
How set-pieces will be refereed differently
The fabric of the laws has not changed but the focus on player behaviour has.
Officials - including in the English Football League and the Women's Super League - will now pay more attention to 'holding actions that have clear material impact'.
The greatest focus will remain on players who are prevented from playing the ball, as that affects the passage of play.
Yet of the 20 missed VAR interventions last season, a quarter were penalties not awarded when a player had been wrestled to the ground off the ball.
So there will be an increased emphasis on those 'non-footballing holding actions that have no place on the football pitch'.
This includes where a player is:
- Only focusing on the opponent (not looking at the ball)
- Making no attempt to play or challenge for the ball
- Holding an opponent with both arms
- Committing sustained and/or impactful holding of an opponent or their clothing
That means a defender who has their back to where a set-piece is coming from and whose only intention is to prevent an attacker's movement will be penalised.
Howard Webb, the Premier League referees' chief, said he wants referees to be more proactive.
"We're trying to get the officials to be as confident as they can be to penalise what they see," Webb said.
"So fewer warnings, more actions penalised, and if there's any reduction in offences being penalised it should be a result of a modification of player behaviour rather than us no longer applying it."
The World Cup saw fewer instances of grappling on corners, with goalkeepers given greater protection.
The Premier League will not be so strict, so do not expect goals to be ruled out if a keeper gets a bump when they are not playing the ball.
"Contact is still part of the game, we still maintain the high threshold," Webb added.
A goalkeeper having the movement of his arm restricted - see Arsenal's David Raya against West Ham - would still be penalised.

Decisions split opinion - even between players at the same club
Every summer Pro Ref, the new name for the referees' body in England, visits each training ground and runs through a series of incidents so players understand what to expect.
Feedback and interaction differs from club to club. Sometimes players will get involved in healthy debates about potential fouls, although on other occasions the odd player might be caught catching a nap.
Over the past few weeks players have been shown clips of two incidents which were not penalties last season, but would be given under the new guidelines.
One was Brentford's Keane Lewis-Potter wrestling West Ham's Tomas Soucek at the far post off the ball. The second was Sunderland's Luke O'Nien dragging down Leeds United's Pascal Struijk with an arm around the neck.
This season, both fall into the category of a 'non-footballing holding action that has no place on the football pitch'.
Webb explained how another incident showed how player opinions "can be split on a grey situation".
Crystal Palace's Marc Guehi was pulled down by Bournemouth's Bafode Diakite, with the referee awarding a spot-kick.
Some players felt Guehi had engineered the contact, others believed it was a clear holding offence.
"One player will tell you that if a penalty is not given, they expect the VAR to be involved, knowing full well that that will highly frustrate the other half of the room, who don't see a penalty in the first place," Webb said.
Webb says giving Guehi the penalty on field was fine, but it should not be a VAR intervention. It shows the balancing act referees and VARs face.
As has been the case for many years, Pro Ref provides officials with pre-game dossiers about how teams play. Not to influence decisions, but to give referees the best chance of identifying potential problems.
"We've got some highly skilled analysts who do a lot of work pre-game and give information to the officials: such as what they're likely to see, the way that the team sets up," Webb said.
"It gives them a higher likelihood of looking in the right place at the right time.
"We'll look at tactics that have been used. We'll look at a team getting an attacking set-piece and adjust the position of the referee to get a beneficial angle.
"It's not about saying this player is a diver and therefore he's going to dive every time he hits the deck.
"An open mind's important, but we think on balance, having information in advance is of benefit."
Who might the winners and losers be?
The Premier League saw 269 goals scored from set-pieces last season - excluding penalties and direct free-kicks.
Set-pieces accounted for a record 25.7% of goals, the highest across Europe's top leagues. The Italian Serie A, on 22.3%, was closest.
The World Cup, with 17.5%, was below all but the French Ligue One, indicating that a stricter approach could impact the effectiveness of set plays.
Webb agrees, arguing that if his referees are stronger, that will influence change.
"If we start penalising offences, players have to adjust their tactics," Webb said. "And then those kind of situations reduce in number.
"But there has been talk on the edges around different approaches that might need to be taken ultimately if tactics continue to develop in a way that makes the game so difficult to officiate."
Arsenal were, of course, the set-piece kings last season with 25 goals scored.
But it was not just about attacking, their seven goals conceded was the fewest in the Premier League too.
Most of the Gunners' success was around well-worked routines, but they were physical at times too.
Manchester United were the second most prolific with 21 goals scored, with Tottenham Hotspur netting 19 despite their poor season.
Maybe it will benefit those who struggled defensively, like Liverpool, who conceded a league-high 19 times from set-pieces, followed by Chelsea and Newcastle on 17.
Law changes and initiatives such as this are met with scepticism.
Clamping down on the worst of the holding to change player behaviour, while still allowing physical contact, is a difficult sweet spot to hit.
Referees are often accused of being strict in the opening weeks, before we drift back to where we were before.
The task is to prove this is not a short-lived policy, and corners and set-pieces can be cleaned up.

Mahatma Gandhi's manuscript sells for ₹16.2 crore at auction, sets record - Check details
The auction house has reportedly confirmed that the buyer is from within India and the manuscript will stay in the country.
In a record-breaking moment for an Indian historical document sold at an auction, a collection of 688 autographed reflections by Mahatma Gandhi has gone ₹16.20 crore at a Saffronart auction to a winning bidder who remains anonymous.
Penned over two years to console and guide his grieving close associate, freedom fighter Anand T. Hingorani, following the death of his wife Vidya, these daily messages were later compiled into a book: “A Thought for the Day.”
Hingorani met Mahatma Gandhi in 1930 and worked at Sabarmati Ashram. He also participated in the Dandi March and joined the Civil Disobedience and Quit India movements, according to a Saffronart press release.

"Gandhi: From the Collection of Anand T Hingorani", featured 86 lots of letters, pictures, manuscripts, and personal objects.
The auction house has also confirmed that “the buyer is from within India and the manuscript will stay in the country, according to news agency PTI.
It further reported that, as per the auction house, the collection addresses various points including truth, ahimsa, brahmacharya, non-possession, religious equality, the removal of untouchability, Ramanama, hunger, duty, Swaraj, non-attachment, the search for God, and several others.
Key auction highlights
1- "Message on God": A set of three related manuscript and correspondence items concerning Mahatma Gandhi's reflections on God and the Bhagavad Gita, sold for ₹1.68 crore (USD 176,842).
2- Personal objects: 'Peti charkha' (box spinning wheel) with two letters on the spiritual discipline of spinning, sold for ₹1.02 crore (USD 107,368).
3- A signed presentation photograph of Mahatma Gandhi writing sold for ₹78 lakh (USD 82,105).
4- A set of letters, telegrams, and postcards focused on economic independence sold for ₹57.60 lakh (USD 60, 632).
According to the report, the collection, preserved by the Hingorani family for decades, offered an intimate perspective on Gandhi.

Saffronart on response to auction
In a statement, Dinesh Vazirani, co-founder, Saffronart, said the response to Lot 80 reinforced its historical significance.
“It has been a privilege to bring the Anand T Hingorani Collection to auction and share a remarkable record of Gandhi’s life and thought. What makes this collection particularly compelling is the opportunity to see one of the most significant figures in India’s history through the lens of a close, personal relationship," Vazirani said.
“The exceptional response to Lot 80—a series of reflections written by Gandhi for Hingorani—reinforces its rarity and historical significance. Together, these reflections offer a rare insight into how Gandhi lived the principles he advocated publicly, making this an especially valuable record of his thought and practice,” the Saffronart co-founder added.

A premium leather bar cabinet in an urban Indian home is more than just a piece of furniture. It reflects a growing shift in how consumers view products that are proudly made in India. For years, premium Indian leather mostly found its way into global brands, while the craftsmanship behind it rarely received the recognition it deserved. Vikash Gupta spent over 15 years on the other side of that story, running a B2B export business that supplied leather goods to international brands. While studying in the US, he also worked part-time at a leather store. It was there that he realised the real gap wasn't in the quality of Indian leather or the skill of its artisans, but in who got credit for the final product. That realisation pushed him to move away from the relatively predictable export business and build a consumer brand of his own. That idea took shape as Three Sixty in 2009, with the belief that handcrafted Indian leather could become a statement piece in modern homes. The opportunity has only grown since then. India's leather goods market touched $14 Bn in 2025 and is expected to reach $20.6 Bn by 2034, driven by rising incomes and growing demand for premium products. The luxury leather segment, in particular, is seeing steady growth as more consumers are willing to spend on high-quality, design-led products. Three Sixty has built its business around balancing traditional craftsmanship with the demands of a modern D2C brand. Many of its artisans have worked with the company for over 25 years, while its "Scalable Craftsmanship" model aims to preserve hand-stitched and hand-finished techniques even as the brand expands across product categories and into Tier II cities such as Bhopal and Patna. Its design philosophy, which blends global aesthetics with Indian leather-craft techniques such as hand-weaving and edge colouring, has also led to collaborations with brands such as Raymond's, BMW, House of Glenfiddich, and Kapil Dev. More than brand partnerships, these collaborations reflect a shared effort to showcase Indian craftsmanship on a larger stage. In a conversation with Inc42, Three Sixty founder Vikash Gupta spoke about his journey from B2B exports to building a premium D2C brand, the thinking behind the brand philosophy of "Live the Leather Life", and his vision of making Three Sixty a global ambassador for Indian leather. Here are the edited excerpts from the conversation... Inc42: You spent 16 years in the predictable B2B exports (Ranvik Exports) segment before launching Three Sixty in 2009. What was the exact operational trigger that made you switch from B2B margins to D2C brand risk? Vikash Gupta: The operational transition was rooted in a personal realisation. While living in the US and working in a leather store to pay for my tuition, I saw premium Indian products selling successfully under international brand names, but with the 'India story' completely erased. That was the trigger. I realised I didn't want to just be an invisible supplier; I wanted to be the architect of a global identity. Moving from B2B to D2C was about reclaiming our narrative and proving that an Indian brand could define luxury on its own terms. Inc42: Premium leather furniture and bar decor is an incredibly niche space in India. What market gap convinced you this could scale, and how do you reconcile the slow rhythm of luxury craftsmanship with the fast-scale demands of a D2C business? Vikash Gupta: The data point is behavioural: we are witnessing the premiumisation of the Indian home. As disposable incomes rise, the Indian consumer is shifting from mass-produced trends to ‘conversation pieces’, products that signify personal taste and heritage. Home entertainment has become the centre of modern social life, and we identified a significant gap for high-quality, leather-centric bar and lifestyle accessories that serve as the anchor for these experiences. We aren't just selling a cabinet; we are selling the setting for the best conversations. As for reconciling craftsmanship with scale, in an era of disposable, fast furniture, our commitment to slow, deliberate craftsmanship is actually our greatest competitive advantage. We don't reconcile these models by compromising on speed; we reconcile them by doubling down on 'Scalable Craftsmanship.' We have built a robust design and supply chain architecture that allows us to maintain the integrity of artisanal skill while scaling our output. We aren't competing for the consumer who wants a quick fix; we are building for the customer who wants a legacy piece. Inc42: How would you describe the 'Live the Leather Life' philosophy, and how does it reflect your own values? Vikash Gupta: 'Live the Leather Life' is about authenticity in an age of imitation. Leather is a character-driven, living material that ages with grace, a concept often lost in a market saturated with synthetic alternatives. Our philosophy is an invitation to educate: we want our customers to understand the difference between disposability and longevity. By organising this industry, we aren't just selling products; we are honouring the resource, the artisan, and the consumer's desire for something real. Inc42: Three Sixty operates in a fairly niche category with products like handcrafted leather furniture, bars, décor and travel accessories. How and when did you realise that this could be a category to build in? Vikash Gupta: My years as a global supply chain partner gave me a unique vantage point: I saw that global brands were building lifestyle ecosystems around leather, not just selling standalone items. I realised that the Indian domestic market was ready for a brand that treated leather not just as a material, but as the centrepiece of home experience. When you see your product being the stage for friendships and celebrations, you realise you aren't just in the furniture business; you are in the experience business. Operating in this supply chain also taught me that the true luxury of leather lies in its longevity and how it evolves with the owner. Unlike mass-produced materials that deteriorate over time, high-quality, handcrafted leather develops a beautiful patina, absorbing the history and character of the home it lives in. By focusing on bespoke bars, tailored decor, and specialised travel accessories, we discovered that our niche wasn't defined by a lack of demand, but by a demand for deeper meaning. Today's conscious consumers aren’t looking for transient trends; they want to invest in enduring, artisanal pieces that carry a distinct soul and tell a story across generations. Inc42: How central is Indian craftsmanship and artisanal skill to the brand's identity, and how do you work with your artisan community? Vikash Gupta: Craftsmanship is the soul of Three Sixty. We have artisans who have been with us for over 25 years; their hands are our institutional memory. For us, ethics isn't a checklist; it's a culture. We prioritise the welfare of our artisans, from banking and financial inclusion to educational support for their children. When I am on the shop floor with them, I'm not just managing production; I am working with the partners who make our India Story possible. Inc42: Tell us more about the design philosophy. How do you balance global design trends with Indian leather craftsmanship? Vikash Gupta: We have a strong in-house design team comprising graduates from NID and NIFT who develop every collection from the ground up. We treat our design division as a research lab. We don't copy; we curate. Our process involves blending global design inspiration with traditional Indian leather techniques, and we encourage our team to travel and collaborate with international designers, bringing those learnings back to the shop floor. The magic happens when the global aesthetic meets the raw, tactile skill of our Indian craftsmen; that synthesis is where every Three Sixty piece is born. This balance is achieved by respecting the strengths of both worlds: global design brings structural discipline, sleek silhouettes, and contemporary functionality, while our local artisans bring soul, texture, and centuries of hand-stitching heritage. We might take a minimalist, mid-century modern frame inspired by European trends and elevate it using intricate traditional Indian hand-weaving or specialised edge-colouring techniques passed down through generations. By treating leather not just as a covering but as a living canvas, our designs tell a story of global sophistication rooted in authentic Indian craftsmanship, ensuring each piece feels at home in a modern metropolitan setting anywhere in the world while retaining its distinct artisanal identity. Inc42: Tell us about the brand's approach to sustainability. Why handcrafted and long-lasting pieces over mass-produced ones? Vikash Gupta: True sustainability is about durability. We have consciously moved away from the fast-fashion mentality that has encroached on the furniture industry. Leather is, by nature, a circular, biodegradable byproduct of the food industry. When handled with expert craftsmanship, it becomes an heirloom meant to be passed down through generations. By focusing on products that last, we are actively reducing the need for constant, wasteful replacements. We are building for longevity, not just for the season. Inc42: Collaborations with Raymond's Chairman's Collection, BMW, House of Glenfiddich and Kapil Dev are notable. How do these partnerships come about, and what do they add to the brand? Vikash Gupta: These partnerships are strategic manifestations of the India Story. Whether it's collaborating with Kapil Dev on his iconic cricket milestones or working with William Grant & Sons for the first time in their 130-year history outside of the liquor industry, these brands choose us because we share a commitment to legacy. We don't look for transactional partnerships; we look for brands that want to co-author a story of excellence and Indian pride. These alliances elevate purpose; they validate handcrafted leather as a premium medium for storytelling. When we designed the limited-edition, signed portable bars celebrating Kapil Dev's legendary 175* knock, or curated immersive interior statements with the House of Glenfiddich, we weren't just creating products; we were designing collectables. Looking ahead, we are exploring deep, multisensory collaborations with visionary creators and luxury lifestyle brands that push the boundaries of where artisanal leather can be found, creating bespoke experiential touchpoints that celebrate design innovation and authentic Indian heritage on both domestic and global stages. Inc42: How would you describe the culture within Three Sixty, especially leadership's relationship with employees and artisans? Vikash Gupta: We are one big family. In a high-growth environment, maintaining an open, human-centric culture is paramount. My leadership style is built on proximity; I believe in spending time on the shop floor because that is where the brand is actually made. When leadership respects the artisans as the true creators, the entire organisation aligns behind the vision of building a global Indian brand. This mutual respect is what transforms our workshop from a production unit into a thriving community. We place a strong emphasis on dignity of labour and continuous upskilling, ensuring our artisans see themselves not just as workers, but as specialised custodians of a rare craft. By bridging the gap between corporate strategy and the shop floor, we create a workplace where a master craftsman's generational knowledge is valued just as highly as a design graduate's fresh perspective. When our team sees that their individual artistry is directly responsible for putting Indian luxury on the global map, it breeds a deep sense of shared ownership and pride that traditional corporate incentives simply cannot replicate. Inc42: Three Sixty has expanded into cities such as Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad, Bhopal, and Patna. What's driving this Tier II expansion strategy? Vikash Gupta: The aspiration in Tier II India is palpable. We are seeing a significant shift where consumers in these cities are demanding the same world-class design and quality as metro dwellers, but with their own distinct preferences. We aren't just expanding footprints; we are tapping into the next wave of Indian luxury. The future of the India Story is being written in these cities, and we intend to be right there as the preferred lifestyle partner. Inc42: What does becoming a 'complete lifestyle ecosystem' mean for Three Sixty's future, and where do you see the brand on the global stage in the next five to ten years? Vikash Gupta: Becoming a complete lifestyle ecosystem means moving from providing furniture to curating environments. We are looking beyond the product. We want to define the spaces in which our customers live, travel, and entertain. We are expanding our design language to ensure that from the moment you wake up to the moment you host a guest, Three Sixty Leather is the thread that ties your lifestyle together. On the global stage, the ambition is clear: ThreeSixty will be the primary global ambassador for Indian leather craftsmanship. My goal is for the brand to sit comfortably in the same conversation as the world's great luxury names, proving that 'Made in India' is synonymous with world-class design, ethical production, and timeless luxury. We are not just building a company; we are cementing India's place in the global luxury discourse.

GitHub says commits have doubled in the last four months
The new traffic peak caused "capacity failures" that led to the developer platform's recent outage.
Following its extended outage on Monday, GitHub says capacity issues — not a code or configuration change — led to several of its services being inaccessible for over seven hours. In the developer platform's own words, "traffic reached a new peak, and a critical infrastructure component in our Central US data center failed to scale with it."
The change in demand that caused the traffic spike is dramatic. "Since April, monthly commits have grown from 1.4 billion to 2.9 billion," GitHub says. "That growth explains the pressure on our systems, but it does not excuse these outages." That means the number of changes being made to projects hosted on the platform has more than doubled in the last four months, a huge uptick in usage that tracks with the growing amount of code that's been produced by AI.
GitHub has a more technical explanation of what went wrong on its status report page, but the biggest fixes the platform is making to avoid future outages are to how it handles simultaneous activity. Specifically, GitHub says it's reviewing CPU and memory alerts to find components in its servers that might fail during periods of high traffic, and it's "applying consistent retry limits, retry budgets, and variable timeouts across service-to-service interactions to prevent retry storms and cascading load."
While those address GitHub's immediate issues, they don't account for the trend that produced the traffic spike in the first place — more and more code is being handed off to AI. With both Anthropic and OpenAI continuing to build on their AI coding tools, the pressure GitHub identified likely isn't going away. As the default home for professional and hobbyist software projects, GitHub is in a position to keep feeling it.

Madrid – Carlos Alcaraz announced on Thursday that he will return at the U.S. Open to defend his title after recovering from a wrist injury that has sidelined him for the past four months.
“I’m back,” the seven-time Grand Slam champion said in a video posted on social media. “Here we go.”
The Spaniard has not played since withdrawing from the Barcelona Open in mid-April with a right wrist injury, missing both the French Open and Wimbledon.
Alcaraz became the youngest man to complete the career Grand Slam in January with his triumph, at age 22, at the Australian Open.
He added the ATP hard court title in Doha in February.
But after withdrawing in Barcelona, he pulled out of tournaments in Madrid and Rome before withdrawing from Roland Garros, where he was the two-time reigning champion.
He pulled the plug on the French Open a month before the tournament and withdrew from Wimbledon almost six weeks before it was scheduled to begin.
His camp has been stingy with details of the injury, reported to be tenosynovitis — in which fluid accumulates in a tendon sheath.
At Wimbledon, rival Jannik Sinner prevailed for the second year in a row, beating French Open winner Alexander Zverev in the final.
In the wake of that victory, Sinner voiced the hope that he would soon renew his rivalry with the Spaniard.
“We hope that Carlos is coming back ... because tennis needs him,” Sinner said.
Zverev moved into No. 2 in the world rankings ahead of Alcaraz after Wimbledon, but Alcaraz has since regained the spot ahead of the German.
Alcaraz had been slated to return for this week’s hard court tournament in Cincinnati, the last big tune-up for the US Open.
When he withdrew, it sparked concerns he wouldn’t be ready to defend his title at Flushing Meadows, but those fears were allayed somewhat when photos of Alcaraz playing practice sets with ATP rival Holger Rune surfaced on social media this week.
Until this year Alcaraz had missed just one Grand Slam since making his main draw debut at the 2021 Australian Open, missing Melbourne in 2023 with a hamstring injury.

Nigeria's mass wedding - and how telling lovers from fraudsters is proving tricky
- Published
Celebrations have turned the northern Nigerian city of Kano into a riot of colour and excitement over the last week as 1,500 couples married at a mass wedding.
For days the city's streets have been buzzing with bridal parties and their families preparing outfits and attending other organised events.
On Friday, brides in red hijabs with grooms in matching red hats and white robes went to the palace of the Emir, the city's traditional Muslim leader, for the main ceremony where they officially became husband and wife.
The nuptials culminated on Saturday with a wedding breakfast hosted by Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf, who offered his blessing to the newlyweds.
The Kano state government sponsored this initiative, spending 1.5bn naira ($1m; £815,000) to support those tying the knot - providing the bride's dowry and furniture for the couple's first home.
The scheme targets low-income individuals who cannot afford the significant financial costs associated with marriage.
The annual event was initiated in 2012 by the then-governor when 100 couples - primarily widows and divorcees - wed at the palace.
The mass weddings have continued under subsequent governors, with numbers expanding each year as demand has grown and included those in polygamous Muslim marriages.
Such is the popularity of the scheme that 5,000 couples applied this year.
The event is always overseen by the Hisbah - the city's Islamic police force - and one of their main tasks is to vet the couples wanting to wed.
Kano has a majority Muslim population and Sharia operates in the state alongside the secular legal system.
Mujahid Aminudeen, deputy commander-general of the Hisbah, admits it is not an easy task.
"Whenever we find out that there's something dubious or fishy about a couple, we disqualify them," he tells the BBC.
He says some couples will go to great lengths to convince the authorities that they are a genuine love match when their eye is more on the benefits on offer.
The state government has spent approximately 1m naira ($735; £544) on each participating couple.
According to the Hisbah, the support package a couple receives includes essential household items needed to establish a new home: beds, mattresses, bedsheets, pillows, furniture and food supplies.
Each bride receives a dowry of 100,000 naira, while a further 100,000 naira is provided as start-up capital to encourage small-scale entrepreneurship and help the couple achieve financial self-reliance after marriage.
All intending couples must undergo comprehensive medical examinations - including tests for HIV, hepatitis, pregnancy and genotype compatibility - before being cleared for the programme.
Aminudeen revealed that some couples had been disqualified after being discovered to have altered their medical test results.
In one case, an intending bride was found to have presented her brother as the groom in an attempt to benefit from the scheme.
Local journalist Yusuf Ali Abdallah, who has covered the mass weddings for years, said Nigeria's struggling economy had been fuelling desperation among the applicants this year.
"As we all know, marriage involves spending money and the country's economy is not bright at the moment," he told the BBC.
"This makes some people desperate to get on this list."
One couple who were already married had even attempted to present themselves as an intending pair before being detected and removed from the programme, he said.
Other charlatans have tried to take advantage of those desperate to get on the sponsored list, which was made public two weeks ago.
One Kano resident, who asked to be anonymous, said he had been asked to pay a bribe to get on the list.
"But to be fair to the organisers, I later found out those who asked me for money were not Hisbah staff," he said.
He and his fiancée failed to be chosen for this August's wedding but he said he would try again next year.
Aminudeen admitted that the Islamic police were aware of such allegations: "We have found that there are some people asking others to pay certain money so they can make the list."
But the Hisbah officer wanted to assure all those wishing to wed in future that the entire process should not cost them a single naira.
"We want to announce to the people of Kano that the whole process is free: from the selection to the medicals and the goods set aside for couples - all are covered by the government."
One of successful grooms, 43-year-old clothes trader Rabiu Yusuf, agreed the process of applying to be married had gone smoothly for him.
"Personally, no-one asked me for anything. I was told the government would sponsor it all," he told the BBC.
His new wife is Aisha Auwal - the couple met as she regularly visited his shop to buy clothes.
Yusuf, who already has five children with his first wife, said he was "very happy and can't wait to start a new life" with his customer-turned-bride.
24 year-old Amina Alhassan echoed his sentiments, adding that she had not encountered any problems when applying to marry 40-year-old Nura Abdullahi.
Their union was first arranged by their families in Dambatta village before they presented themselves to the Hisbah.
"Everything has been free and I want to commend the Kano government for this scheme because without it, many couldn't have afforded to marry due to the high cost of living."
After Saturday's wedding feast, the presentation of the household goods began.
But it will take several more days for the excitement to die down in Kano and as the newlyweds busy themselves with setting up home together.

The Taliban in Afghanistan have launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regional and international powers show a readiness to engage more closely with the repressive regime despite its systematic human rights abuses.
Five years after the Taliban took power, an increasing number of countries are renewing ties or scaling up diplomatic contacts with the hardline Islamists, who seized power in Kabul in 2021 after 20 years of brutal insurgent warfare.
Campaigners fear that the individual contacts by different countries risk undermining “coherent, consistent” demands for an improvement in human rights in return for any diplomatic concessions.
The United Nations described a recent “cascade of [Taliban] edicts and laws” that have banned women from universities and most employment, denied teenage girls education and imposed strict dress codes. Minorities have been persecuted, while activists and journalists face repression. Afghanistan has become a “graveyard for human rights,” the UN said in March.
India, Qatar, China, Iran and several central Asian states all recently welcomed Taliban officials or opened new channels of communication. Russia, which recognised the Taliban government in Kabul just over a year ago, signed a military cooperation agreement last month. In June, the European Union held talks with Taliban officials in Brussels about returning failed asylum-seekers to Afghanistan. Individual European countries have also deepened their own contacts with Kabul.
“There is no doubt there has been an evolution. The Islamic emirate is now in a confident position. They have realised they are indispensable for regional countries right now and even with Europe and the US they have identified how to engage,” said Shivam Shekhawat, at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.
“The Taliban see any kind of contact as a diplomatic win and they have been able to capitalise on that as a sign granting legitimacy to the regime.”
A strict policy of isolation imposed after the Taliban seized power in 2021 towards informal or “de facto” recognition is now fragmenting. Some western commentators have suggested more countries recognise the regime. Others want intensified “back channel” engagement.
“We are not against any engagement … There is a need for engagement even if just for aid agencies to mitigate the ongoing humanitarian crisis but we are worried about the end goal of these contacts and the discussions that are taking place,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“There should be a consistent and coherent message from the international community to the Taliban that they will not have any friends if they do not show real progress in terms of the women’s rights and human rights situation … and that is not happening.”
The new contacts stem from a combination of regional security concerns, pressure in the west to reduce illegal immigration and a general recognition that the Taliban are unlikely to be forced from power in the foreseeable future.
The European Commission downplayed its discussions in Brussels with a Taliban delegation, the first such formal encounter since 2021, as merely “technical” and focused on returns, but a Taliban spokesperson claimed it was a historic visit that was a step towards regularising consular relations with EU countries.
The meeting prompted outrage.
“You cannot condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and then announce talks on immigration in the next … The Taliban are telling their constituency back home that they are now accepted by the international community,” said Abbasi.
This year officials from Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have all visited Kabul or other Afghan cities, seeking trade routes and pipeline deals that would allow their landlocked countries access to seaports or third countries beyond.
India too has moved to reinforce relationships that were frosty after the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, in part to exploit new tensions between the movement and the Islamist movement’s historic sponsors, Pakistan.
New Delhi secured a sanctions waiver last year so that Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban foreign minister and a veteran official who has spent decades at the heart of the movement, could travel there.
In June, India’s UN envoy suggested a rethink was necessary on sanctions, such as travel bans, asset freezes and arms embargoes, that target dozens of Taliban members.
“The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current UN sanctions regime must take that into account,” said Harish Parvathaneni.
Afghan authorities’ diplomatic strategy has involved hosting envoys in Kabul, including those from China, Japan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Last year, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, made the first visit by an Iranian foreign minister to Kabul for almost a decade.
The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan “seeks relations with all countries”, Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said, though “the countries of the region and our neighbouring states have particular importance, because our economic ties and interests are closely linked”.
Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute focusing on Russia’s policy towards the Middle East, said Moscow had multiple reasons for recognising the Taliban regime and seeking closer relations.
“One likely objective is simply having allies … Afghanistan is also very significant for Russia geographically and Russia just wants influence in that part of the world. There was an opening and they were able to take it,” Borshchevskaya said.
“It’s a very cold, cynical calculation. It’s part of a very simple zero-sum view that for Russia to win the US has to lose. From the Kremlin perspective, this is a global battle and whether you are looking at Europe or Afghanistan or wherever, it’s one geopolitical chessboard.”
Britain has said it pursues a policy of “limited and pragmatic” engagement with Taliban officials, largely through the UK Mission to Afghanistan based at the British embassy in Qatar. Discreet meetings with the Taliban have also repeatedly been held by other western countries in Qatar. In Germany and at least four other western European capitals, key consulates are now controlled by the Taliban, not representatives of the former Afghan government.
Taliban officials have also sought cross-border infrastructure projects to boost the country’s fragile economy and diplomacy. Natural resources are another lure for overseas powers. Kabul has expanded the mining sector, attracting firms from neighbouring China and elsewhere.
China, which is worried about Islamic militancy on and around its south-western borders, has welcomed Taliban officials in recent years, and hosted talks when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war earlier this year.
The Taliban are split, with deep disagreements on the ban on women’s education among other issues, but remain dominated by the most conservative factions. Recent laws have further reinforced repression, designating many religious minorities, including Shia Muslims, as heretics and imposing strict punishments to silence dissent.
Other new laws recognise only “excessive” beating as domestic violence against women and facilitate the marriage of girls without their consent. 
Analysts do not believe the Taliban are likely to moderate their position in the near future and point to the continuing authority of Hibatullah Akhundzada, the reclusive and authoritarian cleric leader.
Ramin Mansoori, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Endowment who studies Afghan politics, said the Taliban’s priority was its domestic agenda.
“They are not going to make any significant concessions. Most of them don’t have an international perspective,” Mansoori said.

Walmart shoppers can now worry less about forgetting their wallets in the car.
The company said Friday that it will begin adding tap-to-pay options to its checkout stations at US stores and Sam's Club warehouses, starting August 24 through the remainder of the year. Fuel stations will be upgraded by mid-2027.
This means that shoppers can now use their "eligible contactless card, phone, or smartwatch," and a spokesperson confirmed this includes options like Apple Pay and Google Pay.
Walmart has long been a holdout to NFC-based payments, opting instead for its proprietary Walmart Pay app and Scan and Go app features for contactless payments.
The issue went viral last year when YouTuber MrBeast was flummoxed by the lack of a tap option.
"Younger consumers in particular are so used to using Apple Pay and tap-to-pay with their phones that they're coming to expect it," Emarketer principal retail analyst Sky Canaves told Business Insider at the time. (Emarketer is owned by Axel Springer, Business Insider's parent company.)
Now it looks like Walmart has had a change of heart.
"It all comes back to giving customers and members more choice and making everyday shopping a little easier," the company said.
